## New to networks? Start with these words

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Network | Connected devices exchanging information. |
| Protocol | An agreed set of rules for exchanging messages. |
| Packet | A small addressed piece of information traveling through a network. |
| Frame | A local-delivery wrapper carrying information over one link. |
| IP address | An address used when delivering packets within and between networks. |
| MAC address | An identifier used for local Ethernet delivery. |
| Subnet and prefix | An IP address group and the boundary describing that group, such as /24. |
| Gateway | A router used to reach another network. |
| Interface and port | An interface is a connection. An Ethernet port is a physical socket; a TCP/UDP port number identifies an application conversation. |
| Bit and byte | A bit is 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte. |
| Traffic | The messages moving through a network. |
| Client and server | A client requests a service; a server provides it. |

## Scope and lab assumptions

Use the exam version for your scheduled test. Match command examples to their stated platform, software, license and interfaces. Documentation review is not physical-device validation. The guided CLI and VLAN explorer are educational models; hands-on work belongs in a suitable simulator or supported lab.

Each command block below preserves its source text and platform label. Management-workstation commands are separate from IOS XE commands. Additional concept examples may contain older syntax. A copied configuration needs the lab’s addresses, interfaces, credentials and topology.

CLI reminder: `enable` enters privileged EXEC; `configure terminal` enters global configuration; interface/line commands enter submodes. `end` returns to privileged EXEC. Validate the result, then use `copy running-config startup-config` when saving is appropriate.

## How to use the command examples

The CLI is a text-based control panel. Type one command per line on the device named in the block. A show command normally reads information; configuration commands change active settings.

A prompt ending in &gt; is basic user EXEC access, # is privileged EXEC access, and (config…)# identifies a configuration mode. Do not type the prompt itself. enable enters privileged EXEC; configure terminal enters global configuration. interface … enters interface context; exit moves back one level; end returns to privileged EXEC.

Run show, ping and copy from privileged EXEC unless a block says otherwise. Replace every &lt;PLACEHOLDER&gt;, interface and address with your lab values. Lines starting with ! are comments. Apply blocks on the named devices in order; alternatives are separate labs.

Configuration changes take effect immediately. First verify the intended result, then use copy running-config startup-config when you want those settings retained after reboot. Leaving configuration mode alone does not save them.

## 1.0 Network Fundamentals — 20%

Build the foundation. Understand devices, addressing, and how data moves.

13 objectives · 28 lettered subtopics

<a id="objective-1-1"></a>

### 1.1 — Network component roles

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/commands)

A network is a set of cooperating roles. Follow a packet from an endpoint, through access switching and routing, to an application, and identify which device makes each decision.

#### In everyday language

A network lets devices exchange information. Different devices do different jobs along the way.

**A familiar example:** Opening a company web page can involve your laptop, a Wi-Fi access point, a switch, a router and a server.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Packet | A small addressed piece of information sent across a network. |
| Frame | The wrapper used to carry a packet across one local connection. |
| MAC address | An identifier used to deliver Ethernet frames on a local network. |
| IP address | An address used to identify where packets should go across networks. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Laptop creates a request.** The laptop is an endpoint: a device that sends or receives information.
2. **Switch delivers locally.** A switch uses MAC addresses to choose a local connection. A VLAN is one logical local network.
3. **Router chooses the next network.** A router uses IP addresses and a list of routes to move packets between networks.
4. **Server provides a service.** A server runs the requested application. A firewall checks access rules along the path.

**How to read this:** This is a simplified request path. An access point adds the radio connection; real networks can combine roles in one device.

**Keep this in mind:** A switch connects devices within a local network; a router connects networks.

<a id="topic-1-1-a"></a>

#### 1.1.a — IP routing devices

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.a)

**Start here:** A router chooses the next step toward an IP destination and gives the packet a new local delivery wrapper.

A router uses destination IP and the routing table to choose a next hop between networks. It replaces the incoming link-layer frame when forwarding onto another link; the endpoint IPs normally remain unchanged without NAT or tunneling.

<a id="topic-1-1-b"></a>

#### 1.1.b — Switching at Layer 2 and Layer 3

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.b)

**Start here:** A switch delivers within a VLAN using MAC identifiers. A Layer 3 switch can also perform routing between networks.

Layer 2 switching learns source MAC addresses and forwards by destination MAC within a VLAN. A routing-capable Layer 3 switch can also forward between IP subnets when its interfaces, routing capability and platform support are correctly configured.

<a id="topic-1-1-c"></a>

#### 1.1.c — Application-aware firewalls and intrusion prevention

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.c)

**Start here:** A firewall checks permitted conversations; an inline intrusion-prevention system can stop traffic matching an attack rule.

A next-generation firewall can combine connection state, application identity and security policy. An inline IPS can detect and block matching malicious traffic. Detection or a device label alone does not prove the intended traffic is being prevented.

<a id="topic-1-1-d"></a>

#### 1.1.d — Wireless access-point function

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.d)

**Start here:** An access point supplies the Wi-Fi radio connection. Power, successful wireless login and the wired path must all work.

An AP provides the radio connection for wireless clients and connects their traffic to a distribution network. Authentication, association, radio settings and wired reachability must work together; a powered AP alone does not establish client service.

<a id="topic-1-1-e"></a>

#### 1.1.e — Network and wireless controller roles

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.e)

**Start here:** A controller coordinates devices. Coordination alone does not put every user message through that controller.

Controllers coordinate configuration, policy and monitoring across managed devices. A WLC manages wireless functions; Catalyst Center manages enterprise network workflows. Centralized management does not imply every user packet passes through the controller.

<a id="topic-1-1-f"></a>

#### 1.1.f — User and other endpoint devices

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.f)

**Start here:** Endpoints are the devices people or applications use, including laptops, phones and sensors. Their own network settings matter.

An endpoint originates or consumes application traffic, such as a laptop, phone, camera or sensor. Its address, mask/prefix, selected gateway, DNS and local security policy affect connectivity before network-device configuration is considered.

<a id="topic-1-1-g"></a>

#### 1.1.g — Application and infrastructure servers

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.g)

**Start here:** A server provides a service. Being able to reach its address does not prove that the requested application is running.

Servers offer services such as web applications, DNS, DHCP and file storage. A working IP path does not prove the application is listening or authorized. Diagnose the specific service, transport and return path rather than assuming all server functions share one outcome.

<a id="topic-1-1-h"></a>

#### 1.1.h — Delivering power over Ethernet

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.1/1.1.h)

**Start here:** PoE sends power through compatible Ethernet cabling. Check both the port limit and the total switch power allowance.

PoE power-sourcing equipment supplies compatible powered devices over Ethernet cabling. Verify the negotiated standard, cable, per-port capability and total power budget. A switch can have a working data path while insufficient power prevents an AP or phone from operating.

#### Objective overview

- Routers forward packets between IP networks using destination IP addresses and routing tables. Layer 2 switches forward frames inside a VLAN using destination MAC addresses; Layer 3 switches can also route.
- Next-generation firewalls inspect traffic using state and application context. An IPS detects and can block malicious traffic inline. Access points bridge wireless clients to a wired distribution network; controllers centralize AP policy and management.
- Endpoints initiate or consume services; servers provide applications, DNS, DHCP, or files. Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) manages enterprise networks. PoE supplies power and data on Ethernet: a power sourcing device must have enough per-port and total power budget.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 1, 3](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 10, 18](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Follow the protocol layers

**Start here:** A network message is wrapped in several layers, like a letter inside envelopes. Each wrapper supplies information for a different job: local delivery, travel between networks or application delivery.

The OSI layers are physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. TCP/IP groups these into link, internet, transport and application functions. Application data travels inside transport segments/datagrams, IP packets and link frames; each layer serves the layer above it.

##### Identify the forwarding boundary

**Start here:** Ask which decision a device makes. A switch chooses a local port; a router chooses the next network; a firewall checks rules. Power over Ethernet is a separate electrical dependency.

A switch learns and forwards inside a VLAN. A router chooses an IP next hop and creates an outgoing frame. A firewall applies policy using state and context; an inline IPS can stop matching threats. PoE requires both adequate per-port capability and sufficient total switch power budget.

##### Worked review check

What destination MAC does a host use when sending IPv4 to a remote subnet?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

The host uses its local gateway's MAC address, found with ARP, the local IPv4-to-MAC lookup protocol. The outer Ethernet frame is delivered to that gateway, while the IP packet inside still names the remote host as its final destination.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Identify devices and operate switch power delivery.

**Covered features:** 1.1a Routers; 1.1b Layer 2/3 switches; 1.1c Firewalls and IPS; 1.1d APs; 1.1e Controllers; 1.1f Endpoints; 1.1g Servers; 1.1h PoE.

##### Identify the hardware, software and neighbors

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Read the device's identity, then compare the local-delivery directory with the network route list.

Inventory identifies the device; routing and MAC tables show different forwarding roles. A Catalyst Center appliance, NGFW/IPS, endpoint or server has its own operating interface; these switch commands do not configure those products.

```text
show version
show inventory
show cdp neighbors detail
show lldp neighbors detail
show ip route
show mac address-table
```


##### Enable automatic PoE negotiation

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**Objective coverage:** 1.1h

**In plain language:** Let a compatible powered port negotiate power; check that the switch still has enough watts available.

Automatic PoE negotiates power with a connected powered device. This requires a PoE-capable physical port and sufficient switch power budget.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5
 description Wireless_AP
 power inline auto
 no shutdown
end
```


**Expected result:** show power inline reports an operational powered device and its allocated wattage.

##### Check power and controller/AP membership

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x / Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

**In plain language:** Check power on the switch and wireless membership on the controller; these are different device views.

Use the matching platform. A switch reports its port/power; a WLC reports AP and client membership.

```text
! Switch privileged EXEC
show power inline
show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/5 status
! Run on the Catalyst 9800 instead:
show ap summary
show wireless client summary
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- No power: check PoE hardware, total budget, cabling, port state and device compatibility.
- Do not use power inline never unless deliberately removing power from the device.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** Follow each arrow as the request moves toward the server. PoE means the Ethernet cable can also supply power to a compatible device.

```text
Path: laptop → AP → access switch → default-gateway router → firewall → application server.
PoE troubleshooting: verify the port supplies power, the device standard, and the switch power budget.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which device normally forwards a frame inside one VLAN using a MAC address table?

- **A.** Layer 2 switch
- **B.** DNS server
- **C.** Wireless client
- **D.** Router routing process

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. Layer 2 switch**

A Layer 2 switch keeps a local directory of MAC addresses and ports. It learns where senders are heard, then uses the receiver's destination MAC to choose the outgoing port within that VLAN.

</details>

<a id="objective-1-2"></a>

### 1.2 — Network topology architectures

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/commands)

Topology describes how devices connect; architecture describes where functions and failure boundaries live.

#### In everyday language

A network design describes how devices connect and where responsibilities are placed.

**A familiar example:** A small office can combine several jobs in one box. A large campus often separates those jobs so a failure affects fewer people.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Topology | The arrangement of devices and connections. |
| Access layer | The part where user devices connect. |
| Distribution layer | The part that gathers access connections and applies policy. |
| Core | The fast, reliable connection between distribution areas. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Connect people.** Access switches connect laptops, phones and other devices.
2. **Gather connections.** Distribution connects groups of access switches. A two-tier design combines this role with the core.
3. **Join larger areas.** A separate core connects distribution areas in a three-tier design.

**How to read this:** These are functional roles, not a requirement for exactly three physical switches. In a spine–leaf design, every leaf connects to every spine instead.

**Keep this in mind:** Count roles rather than boxes. Cloud services also divide responsibilities between you and the provider.

<a id="topic-1-2-a"></a>

#### 1.2.a — Collapsed-core campus layout

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.a)

**Start here:** Two-tier means access connections plus combined distribution/core functions. It does not mean exactly two switches.

A two-tier campus combines distribution and core functions in a collapsed core while keeping access connectivity separate. Identify its aggregation paths and failure boundaries instead of counting every switch as a separate tier.

<a id="topic-1-2-b"></a>

#### 1.2.b — Access, distribution and core tiers

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.b)

**Start here:** Three-tier separates user connections, aggregation/policy and a resilient backbone into three roles.

A three-tier campus separates endpoint access, aggregation/policy and resilient core transit. The design supports scale and failure isolation; its tier names describe roles rather than mandatory switch models.

<a id="topic-1-2-c"></a>

#### 1.2.c — Leaf-to-spine fabric layout

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.c)

**Start here:** Every leaf connects to every spine. Different leaves normally communicate through one spine rather than a direct leaf-to-leaf cable.

Each leaf connects to each spine, creating predictable paths between leaves and possible equal-cost forwarding. Server-to-server traffic between leaves normally crosses a spine; adding leaf-to-leaf links is not the defining topology.

<a id="topic-1-2-d"></a>

#### 1.2.d — Connectivity between distant sites

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.d)

**Start here:** A WAN joins distant sites through another network provider or the Internet. Private service does not automatically mean encrypted service.

A WAN joins geographically separated networks through provider or Internet services. Distinguish the delivered Layer 2/Layer 3 service, availability and routing responsibilities. A provider VPN does not automatically imply encryption.

<a id="topic-1-2-e"></a>

#### 1.2.e — Small-office and home-office layout

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.e)

**Start here:** A small-office/home-office box can combine switching, routing, Wi-Fi and filtering while those remain separate logical jobs.

SOHO equipment often combines routing, switching, wireless, NAT and security in one unit. The same logical roles still exist, even when the topology uses few physical devices.

<a id="topic-1-2-f"></a>

#### 1.2.f — Local infrastructure and cloud services

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.2/1.2.f)

**Start here:** On-premises means operated at your site; cloud uses provider resources. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS give the provider progressively more of the system to operate.

On-premises and cloud describe deployment and operating responsibility. Consider ownership, provisioning, connectivity and shared responsibility. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe service boundaries rather than a universal physical topology.

#### Objective overview

- A two-tier campus combines core and distribution into a collapsed core. A three-tier campus separates access, distribution, and core, improving scaling and fault isolation.
- Spine–leaf designs connect each leaf to every spine for predictable east–west paths in a data center. Traffic between leaves normally crosses one spine; leaves do not need direct links to each other.
- WANs join distant sites through provider or Internet services. SOHO networks combine functions in fewer devices. On-premises infrastructure is operated locally; cloud designs use remotely provisioned resources and shared-responsibility models.
- With IaaS, the provider supplies infrastructure such as virtual compute, storage and networking; the customer normally installs and maintains guest operating systems and applications. PaaS supplies a managed application platform with more of that system maintenance handled by the provider. SaaS exposes a finished application. Identify the service boundary before assigning patching, identity and data-protection responsibilities.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 3](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 18, 19, 20, 21](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Compare paths and failure domains

**Start here:** Follow where a user connects, where connections gather and how large areas join. A failure boundary is the part of the network affected when one component breaks.

Access connects endpoints, distribution aggregates and applies policy, and core supplies resilient transit. A collapsed core combines distribution/core. In spine–leaf, each leaf connects to every spine, giving consistent inter-leaf hop counts and possible equal-cost paths.

##### Distinguish service responsibility

**Start here:** A connection service and a cloud service model answer different questions. One describes how sites connect; the other describes who operates which parts of an application system.

Metro Ethernet may supply Layer 2 connectivity; an MPLS provider may supply a routed VPN. Neither service name promises encryption. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe service responsibilities, while Internet VPNs and private WANs describe ways to reach a service.

##### Worked review check

Does private addressing alone protect inter-site traffic over an Internet replacement for an MPLS WAN?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. A private address is an addressing choice, not encrypted protection. For the Internet path, plan suitable VPN encryption, working routes in both directions, availability and rules deciding which traffic may cross.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Observe an architecture; no single command creates a campus or a cloud.

**Covered features:** 1.2a Two-tier; 1.2b Three-tier; 1.2c Spine–leaf; 1.2d WAN; 1.2e SOHO; 1.2f On-premises/cloud.

##### Map physical and routed paths

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x or IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Compare neighbor information and route tests to build a useful connection map.

Build a diagram from neighbors and interface descriptions, then compare the routed path. Traceroute can reveal Layer 3 hops, not every Layer 2 device or a cloud provider’s internal topology.

```text
show cdp neighbors detail
show lldp neighbors detail
show interfaces description
show ip route
traceroute 192.0.2.80
```


##### Document a link’s role

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Write a human-readable label on the port; the label does not rewire or reconfigure its connection.

An interface description labels intent; it does not change topology, VLAN membership or a cloud deployment.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 description Uplink_to_distribution_SW2
end
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Compare the observed path with your diagram. Redundant links may be blocked by STP or bundled by EtherChannel.
- Spine–leaf, WAN provisioning and cloud networking require design and platform-specific configuration.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The arrows show example paths. In spine–leaf, a server on one leaf normally reaches another leaf through a spine; the picture is not a complete wiring plan.

```text
Two-tier: access → collapsed core
Three-tier: access → distribution → core
Spine–leaf: server → leaf → spine → leaf → server
```


#### Check your understanding

Which architecture connects every leaf switch to every spine switch?

- **A.** Three-tier campus
- **B.** Spine–leaf
- **C.** Daisy chain
- **D.** SOHO

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Spine–leaf**

In spine–leaf, every leaf has a connection to every spine. A server on one leaf can normally reach a server on another through one spine, giving a predictable path pattern.

</details>

Next objective: [1.3 Physical interfaces and cabling](#objective-1-3)

<a id="objective-1-3"></a>

### 1.3 — Physical interfaces and cabling

**Exam target:** Compare.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.3/commands)

Select media by distance, bandwidth, environment, and transceiver compatibility. A connector alone does not identify the supported speed or optical wavelength.

#### In everyday language

A network cable must carry the right kind of signal far enough for both connected devices.

**A familiar example:** A connector that fits is like a plug that fits a socket: it does not prove the equipment supports the same signal.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Copper | Cable carrying electrical signals. |
| Fiber | Cable carrying light signals. |
| Transceiver | The plug-in part that sends and receives a particular cable signal. |
| Duplex | Whether both ends can send at the same time or must take turns. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Check the distance.** Cable and signal standards specify how far the link can reach.
2. **Match both ends.** Choose compatible speed, fiber type, light wavelength and transceivers.
3. **Test the connection.** Check link status and new errors, not just whether the connector fits.

**How to read this:** This is a cable-selection checklist. Copper can suffer electrical interference; fiber does not carry its data as electricity.

**Keep this in mind:** Match the complete standard at both ends, including the cable.

<a id="topic-1-3-a"></a>

#### 1.3.a — Copper, multimode and single-mode media

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.3/1.3.a)

**Start here:** Copper carries electricity; fiber carries light. Match the cable, supported distance and sending/receiving optics at both ends.

Copper uses electrical signals and depends on category, pairs, length and interference. Multimode fiber commonly serves shorter optical links; single-mode supports longer reaches with suitable optics. Match wavelength, transceiver, fiber type and optical budget rather than connector appearance alone.

<a id="topic-1-3-b"></a>

#### 1.3.b — Shared and point-to-point Ethernet links

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.3/1.3.b)

**Start here:** Older shared links take turns and can collide. A modern full-duplex switch link lets its two ends send simultaneously.

Shared half-duplex Ethernet has collision behavior; modern switched full-duplex point-to-point links do not normally have collisions. Each switch port is a separate physical segment, while VLANs define broadcast scope.

#### Objective overview

- Copper twisted pair uses electrical signals and is susceptible to interference. Common balanced-copper Ethernet channels have a 100 m maximum; category and Ethernet standard determine supported speeds.
- Multimode fiber commonly serves shorter optical links; single-mode supports longer distances with a smaller core. Match fiber type, optical wavelength, transceiver standard, connectors, and receive power.
- Point-to-point Ethernet connects two interfaces. Shared media can create collision domains in half duplex; a switch port running full duplex has no collisions. Fiber has separate transmit and receive strands in common duplex designs.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 2, 7](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 18](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read the physical standard

**Start here:** A copper cable contains wire pairs. Some Ethernet standards need two pairs, while gigabit copper needs four; a damaged extra pair can explain why only the lower speed works.

Common 10BASE-T/100BASE-TX links use two twisted pairs; 1000BASE-T uses four. Auto-MDIX adapts transmit/receive pair arrangements on supported ports. Fiber choice also depends on wavelength, optical budget, distance, connectors and transceiver compatibility.

##### Read an Ethernet frame

**Start here:** An Ethernet frame has sender/receiver MAC labels, a type label, its content and a corruption check. The check can detect damage but cannot repair it.

A frame carries destination/source MACs, type/length, payload and FCS. MAC addresses are 48 bits. Common EtherTypes are 0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6 and 0x0806 for ARP. FCS detects corruption; it does not repair the frame.

##### Worked review check

Why might a copper link work at 100 Mb/s but fail at 1 Gb/s?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

100BASE-TX needs two wire pairs, while 1000BASE-T needs all four. A fault in one of the additional pairs can leave 100 Mb/s working but prevent gigabit operation. Inspect all pairs and their connector terminations before assuming an IP configuration problem.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Inspect media and configure supported link parameters.

**Covered features:** 1.3a Single-mode/multimode/copper; 1.3b Point-to-point/shared media.

##### Inspect copper and transceiver state

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Inspect the actual cable interface and supported optical readings; copper ports do not have optical light measurements.

Check actual port type, negotiated speed and optical diagnostics. Transceiver diagnostics are available only on supported optics/ports; a copper port may not report optical values.

```text
show interfaces status
show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1
show interfaces transceiver detail
show inventory
```


##### Use autonegotiation on a supported copper port

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Let supported copper ports agree on speed and simultaneous sending; do not force copper settings onto fixed optical ports.

Copper speed/duplex capabilities depend on the port. Many high-speed fiber ports have fixed characteristics and reject these copper-specific commands.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 speed auto
 duplex auto
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Use interface-mode speed ? and duplex ? to discover supported options.
- A CLI command cannot convert multimode fiber to single-mode or fix wrong Tx/Rx polarity. Replace or recable the physical media correctly.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** Tx means transmit and Rx means receive. Common two-strand fiber links connect the transmitter at one end to the receiver at the other.

```text
Before replacing a link: verify speed → optic type → fiber mode → Tx/Rx polarity → cleanliness → distance.
A 10GBASE-SR optic generally uses multimode fiber; LR generally uses single-mode.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which medium is generally preferred for a long-distance optical link?

- **A.** Unshielded twisted pair
- **B.** Single-mode fiber
- **C.** Console rollover cable
- **D.** Coaxial bus

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Single-mode fiber**

Single-mode fiber is designed for longer optical distances with compatible long-reach transceivers. The cable and both end devices must support the same optical standard; the connector fitting is not enough.

</details>

Next objective: [1.4 Interface and cable faults](#objective-1-4)

<a id="objective-1-4"></a>

### 1.4 — Interface and cable faults

**Exam target:** Identify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.4/commands)

Start at the physical layer and compare both ends of a link before changing configuration.

#### In everyday language

A connection can be switched off, physically broken or overloaded. Those need different fixes.

**A familiar example:** An empty power socket, a damaged cable and a crowded road all stop useful work for different reasons.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | A device connection, such as an Ethernet port. |
| CRC error | A received frame failed its corruption check. |
| Autonegotiation | Both ends agree on supported link settings. |
| Discard | Traffic deliberately dropped, sometimes because a queue is full. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Check whether it is enabled.** Administratively down means configuration has turned the interface off.
2. **Check both ends.** Inspect power, cable and compatible speed/duplex settings.
3. **Compare new errors.** Generate a controlled test and see which counters increase. Old totals can describe an earlier problem.

**How to read this:** Read the steps as a troubleshooting order. An up link proves only part of the path; it does not prove an application works.

**Keep this in mind:** Check what changed during the test before choosing a repair.

#### Build your understanding

- An interface that is administratively down needs no shutdown. Down/down often points to cable, power, optics, or a disabled remote interface. Up/down can indicate a data-link problem.
- CRC or input errors suggest corrupted frames caused by media faults, interference, or a duplex problem. Late collisions commonly point to a half/full duplex mismatch or an invalid collision-domain length.
- Check speed and duplex on both ends. Modern Ethernet typically uses autonegotiation; forcing only one end can introduce mismatches. Discards may indicate congestion rather than physical damage.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 7, 16, 20](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Read both interface states

**Start here:** First distinguish turned off by configuration from unable to detect a physical connection. A working cable still does not prove the next network or application is reachable.

Administratively down indicates a configured shutdown. Physical down points first to cable, power, optics or remote state. Physical-up/line-protocol-down requires checking the interface’s link-layer behavior. A clean link does not prove that an IP route exists.

##### Compare new counter growth

**Start here:** Write down counters before a test, then compare afterward. Corrupted incoming frames suggest different causes from outgoing traffic dropped because too much was waiting.

Record a baseline, generate controlled traffic and inspect new CRCs, collisions, input errors or output drops. Historical counters can describe an old fault. Compare both endpoints and negotiation; normal full-duplex switched Ethernet does not have collisions.

##### Worked review check

Output drops increase while CRCs and collisions stay stable. What should be investigated?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Investigate too much outgoing traffic for the available link or queue. Output drops mean packets could not be sent; stable CRC and collision counters provide less support for damaged media. Compare offered traffic, link speed and queue counters during a fresh test.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Find the fault before changing the interface.

**Covered features:** Collisions; CRC/input errors; Duplex mismatch; Speed mismatch.

##### Inspect operational state and error counters

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Read both status lines and compare newly increasing errors at each end.

Compare both ends. CRC/input errors point toward corruption; output drops may indicate congestion. Administratively down is a different condition from down/down.

```text
show interfaces status
show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1
show interfaces counters errors
show logging | include LINK|LINEPROTO|ERR
```


##### Enable the port and restore supported negotiation

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Enable the intended port and use compatible link settings after checking power and cabling.

Use this after confirming the peer, cabling and intended settings. It does not repair bad copper, dirty fiber or an incompatible transceiver.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 no shutdown
 speed auto
 duplex auto
end
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Compare new counter growth over time rather than interpreting one old cumulative value.
- For an err-disabled port, resolve the security or protocol violation first; merely enabling it can repeat the fault.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The show commands inspect status without configuring the port. Look for both interface states and newly increasing error or drop counters.

```text
show interfaces gigabitEthernet 0/1
show interfaces status
! Compare negotiated speed, duplex, input errors, CRCs and drops.
```


#### Check your understanding

A port shows many CRC errors. What should you investigate first?

- **A.** DNS recursion
- **B.** Cable or physical-link integrity
- **C.** OSPF router ID
- **D.** DHCP lease time

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Cable or physical-link integrity**

A CRC error means a received Ethernet frame failed its corruption check. Start with cable/optical integrity and compatible link settings at both ends, then see whether new errors still appear.

</details>

Next objective: [1.5 TCP and UDP](#objective-1-5)

<a id="objective-1-5"></a>

### 1.5 — TCP and UDP

**Exam target:** Compare.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.5/commands)

Transport protocols identify applications using ports. Choose a protocol based on delivery requirements, not the assumption that one is always faster.

#### In everyday language

Transport protocols help applications exchange data. TCP keeps track of delivery and order; UDP leaves those jobs to the application if needed.

**A familiar example:** A file download needs missing pieces resent. A live call may prefer a short gap over waiting for old audio.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Port number | A number identifying an application conversation, not a physical cable socket. |
| Acknowledgment | A message confirming receipt. |
| Retransmission | Sending missing information again. |
| Handshake | An opening exchange used to establish a connection. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Client sends SYN.** The client asks to start a TCP connection.
2. **Server sends SYN-ACK.** The server agrees and acknowledges the request.
3. **Client sends ACK.** The client confirms. The connection can now carry its application exchange.

**How to read this:** The three steps describe TCP setup. UDP does not use this TCP handshake; an application using UDP can still add its own reliability.

**Keep this in mind:** TCP and UDP describe delivery behavior, not a guarantee of speed or encryption.

#### Build your understanding

- TCP is connection oriented: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK establishes a session. Sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control provide reliable ordered delivery.
- UDP is connectionless and has a smaller header. It does not itself guarantee delivery, order, or retransmission; applications may add those functions.
- DNS commonly uses UDP 53 for queries and TCP 53 when needed, including zone transfers. HTTPS commonly uses TCP 443; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. Voice often favors UDP to avoid waiting for retransmission.
- DHCPv4 clients use UDP port 68 and send requests toward server UDP port 67; servers reply from 67 toward client 68. HTTPS is not limited to one transport: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TLS over TCP 443, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, commonly UDP 443. A TCP-only access rule can therefore exclude that HTTP/3 path.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 1](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 5](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Identify a flow and its reliability

**Start here:** IP addresses identify the devices; transport port numbers identify application conversations. TCP tracks delivered bytes and controls how much the receiver must accept at once.

IP addresses, transport protocol and source/destination ports identify a transport flow. Clients often use ephemeral source ports. TCP sequence/acknowledgment numbers track bytes and its receive window supplies flow control. UDP itself supplies neither retransmission nor ordered delivery.

##### Learn behavior with port numbers

**Start here:** Learn common service numbers with their transport. TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different matching choices even though DNS can use both; a number alone does not prove the application identity.

Recognize SSH TCP 22, HTTP TCP 80, HTTPS TCP 443, DNS TCP/UDP 53, DHCP UDP 67/68, NTP UDP 123, SNMP UDP 161/162, FTP TCP 21 and initial TFTP UDP 69. A port alone does not prove the application actually running.

##### Worked review check

Why can allowing only TCP 443 block a modern HTTPS client?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Some modern HTTPS uses HTTP/3 over QUIC, carried by UDP, commonly port 443. A rule permitting only TCP 443 matches a different transport and does not allow that UDP path. Permit only the intended transports explicitly.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Observe transport behavior; applications select TCP or UDP.

**Covered features:** TCP handshake/reliability; UDP delivery; Application ports.

##### Inspect device-local transport sessions

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Inspect connections belonging to the network device itself; this does not show every conversation passing through it.

These commands describe sessions or listeners associated with the device itself. They are not a capture of all transit TCP/UDP traffic, and command support varies by platform.

```text
show tcp brief all
show udp
show control-plane host open-ports
```


##### See transport matching in an extended ACL

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Read protocol and application-port matches in a rule, then check where that rule is applied.

Read the protocol and port fields together with the interface attachment. To observe the actual three-way handshake, capture traffic in a lab using Wireshark or supported Embedded Packet Capture.

```text
show ip access-lists
show ip interface GigabitEthernet1
show running-config | section ip access-list
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A ping tests ICMP reachability, not whether a TCP application accepts connections.
- Do not invent a TCP/UDP enable command: transport selection belongs to the application.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** Read right-pointing arrows as client-to-server and left-pointing arrows as server-to-client. SYN starts synchronization; ACK acknowledges it.

```text
TCP handshake:
Client → SYN → Server
Client ← SYN-ACK ← Server
Client → ACK → Server
```


#### Check your understanding

Which function is supplied by TCP but not by UDP itself?

- **A.** IP addressing
- **B.** Reliable ordered byte-stream delivery
- **C.** MAC learning
- **D.** Route selection

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Reliable ordered byte-stream delivery**

TCP numbers the bytes it sends, checks acknowledgments and resends missing data. These mechanisms provide ordered, reliable delivery. UDP itself does not provide them, although an application can add similar checks.

</details>

Next objective: [1.6 IPv4 addresses and subnetting](#objective-1-6)

<a id="objective-1-6"></a>

### 1.6 — IPv4 addresses and subnetting

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.6) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/1.6/commands)

An IPv4 address is 32 bits. A prefix separates network bits from host bits; devices compare their own prefix to the destination to decide whether to use a gateway.

#### In everyday language

An IPv4 address has a network part and a device part. The /number tells you how many of its 32 binary digits belong to the network part.

**A familiar example:** Think of a subnet as one street and a device address as one house on that street. This analogy helps with grouping; real addresses use binary arithmetic.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Bit | A single binary digit: 0 or 1. |
| Prefix | The fixed network part, written as /26 for 26 network bits. |
| Subnet mask | The same boundary written in dotted form. |
| Broadcast address | An address representing all IPv4 hosts on an ordinary local subnet. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Count the remaining bits.** For /26, 32 − 26 = 6 bits remain for addresses within the block.
2. **Find the block.** 2 to the power of 6 is 64. Last-octet blocks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192.
3. **Place the address.** 77 is between 64 and 127. The network is .64 and broadcast is .127.
4. **Find ordinary host addresses.** Exclude those two endpoints: .65 through .126, giving 62 host addresses.

**How to read this:** Use the shared first three address numbers 192.168.10 for this example. The /31 point-to-point and /32 single-host exceptions are explained in the detailed material.

**Keep this in mind:** First find the block; then separate its network, broadcast and ordinary host addresses.

#### Build your understanding

- A /24 has 24 network bits and 8 host bits. The mask is 255.255.255.0. Traditional usable-host count is 2^(32-prefix) − 2 for network and broadcast addresses.
- Find subnet boundaries with the block size: 256 minus the interesting mask octet. A /26 mask ends in 192, so the block size is 64: networks begin at .0, .64, .128, .192.
- VLSM allocates differently sized subnets: allocate the largest host requirement first, then keep every network aligned to its prefix boundary. /31 point-to-point links use both addresses; /32 identifies a single host route.
- A subnet mask has consecutive network one-bits followed by host zero-bits. The octet weights are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, so four network bits in the last octet give 128+64+32+16=240. To derive a subnet, keep its network bits and clear the host bits; set those host bits to one for its broadcast address. On an ordinary LAN, the usable range lies between those two addresses and a host gateway must be a usable address on the same link. Apply the separately stated /31 and /32 exceptions where appropriate.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Plan from requirements

**Start here:** Start with the required number of devices. Keep enough host bits so the address block fits them, including the ordinary network and broadcast addresses that hosts cannot use.

Calculate prefix, dotted mask, network, broadcast and host range. For ordinary LANs, choose host bits h so 2^h − 2 meets the requirement. Class A/B/C masks supply historical context; they do not override an explicit CIDR prefix. /31 and /32 require their special interpretations.

##### Work a VLSM allocation

**Start here:** Allocate the largest group first. In this example, blocks of 128, 64 and 32 addresses fit 100, 50 and 20 ordinary hosts without giving the same address to two groups.

Inside 192.168.50.0/24, allocate 100 hosts as 192.168.50.0/25, 50 as 192.168.50.128/26 and 20 as 192.168.50.192/27. Each subnet is aligned, inside its parent and nonoverlapping. 192.168.50.224/27 remains available.

##### Worked review check

What is the longest equal-subnet prefix for at least 500 traditional usable hosts per subnet of 172.16.0.0/16?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

1. Try nine host bits: 2^9 − 2 = 510 ordinary usable addresses, enough for 500. 2. Keep 32 − 9 = 23 network bits, giving /23. 3. The original /16 leaves 23 − 16 = 7 subnet bits, so there are 2^7 = 128 equal subnets. /24 would supply only 254 hosts.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Configure an IPv4 subnet on a routed interface.

**Covered features:** IPv4 address/mask; Subnet boundaries; VLSM; Verification.

##### Assign the address and enable the link

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Give the gateway an address in the planned block and enable its physical connection.

This /26 contains network .64, usable hosts .65–.126 and broadcast .127. Configure a client as .66/26 with gateway .65.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 description LAN_192.168.10.64_26
 ip address 192.168.10.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
end
```


**Expected result:** The interface is up/up; the routing table contains connected 192.168.10.64/26 and local 192.168.10.65/32.

##### Verify the subnet and local host

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Read the full mask and confirm a local host can reach the gateway; a short status listing may hide the mask.

Check both address and mask: brief output omits the mask. On a multilayer switch, use a routed port with no switchport, or an SVI as in lesson 2.1.

```text
show ip interface brief
show ip interface GigabitEthernet1
show ip route connected
show ip arp
ping 192.168.10.66
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- If the interface is down, a connected route may not install. Check physical/line protocol state.
- VLSM is a design calculation: assign aligned, nonoverlapping subnets before configuring addresses.

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
