**Start here:** One-host routes and wider network routes cover different destination sets. An IPv6 local-link next hop also needs an interface to identify which link you mean.

IPv4 host routes use /32; IPv6 host routes /128. A link-local IPv6 next hop needs an outgoing interface. On multiaccess Ethernet an exit-only route can create per-destination ARP/proxy-ARP behavior; a reachable next-hop address or fully specified form is usually clearer.

##### Understand backup limits

**Start here:** A floating backup stays less preferred while the main route is available. A faraway outage may not remove the main route, so preference numbers alone cannot detect every failure.

A floating route needs a higher AD than the preferred route to the same prefix. It activates when the primary is withdrawn or unresolved. A remote failure can leave the primary next hop reachable, requiring tracking in a real design. The backup path also needs a return route.

##### Worked review check

Will a static route AD 5 float behind OSPF AD 110 for the same prefix?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. Lower AD is preferred, so the static route at 5 would beat OSPF at 110 for the same prefix. Choose a backup value above 110, such as 200, and verify the alternative next hop and reply path work.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Configure defaults, network routes, host routes and floating backups.

**Covered features:** IPv4/IPv6; Default; Network; Host; Floating static.

##### Configure IPv4 route variants

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Choose the IPv4 route form and a higher backup AD for the same destination block.

The route with AD 200 is a backup for the same /16. It installs only when lower-AD candidates disappear; it does not track end-to-end Internet health by itself.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.0.2.2
ip route 192.0.2.80 255.255.255.255 192.0.2.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.1
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 198.51.100.2 200
end
```


##### Configure IPv6 route variants

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Include the interface when the IPv6 next hop has only local-link scope.

A link-local next hop needs its egress interface to disambiguate the link. Replace it with reachable neighbors on that interface.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::80/128 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::2
ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::1
! A separate reachable backup link; AD 200 floats above AD 1.
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet2 fe80::2 200
end
```


##### Check installation and next-hop reachability

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Check both route installation and a working return path.

Verify both forward and return routing before testing an application.

```text
show ip route static
show ipv6 route static
show ip route 10.20.0.1
show ipv6 neighbors
ping 192.0.2.2
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- An Ethernet exit-interface-only static route can produce undesirable per-destination ARP behavior; use a suitable next hop.
- A high-AD route remaining absent is expected while the primary route is installed.
- A higher AD alone does not detect a remote failure when the primary next hop stays resolvable. Production failover may need tracking and a validated return path.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The lines are separate examples: a network route, IPv4 default, higher-AD backup, and IPv6 default. The final 200 sets the backup AD; the IPv6 interface identifies the link containing fe80::1.

```text
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.0.2.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.1
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 198.51.100.2 200
ipv6 route ::/0 g0/0 fe80::1
! show ip route static
```


#### Check your understanding

What makes a static route a floating backup?

- **A.** A lower prefix length
- **B.** An AD higher than the primary route
- **C.** A multicast next hop
- **D.** A loopback source

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. An AD higher than the primary route**

A floating route has a higher administrative distance than the preferred route for the same destination block. It stays less preferred while the primary is available and can become usable after the primary route disappears.

</details>

Next objective: [3.4 Single-area OSPFv2](#objective-3-4)

<a id="objective-3-4"></a>

### 3.4 — Single-area OSPFv2

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/commands)

OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. Routers discover neighbors, synchronize a link-state database and calculate shortest paths using interface costs.

#### In everyday language

OSPF lets routers share a map of network links and calculate paths. Routers must agree on key settings before exchanging that map.

**A familiar example:** Two people comparing maps need to agree which region and roads they are discussing.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Neighbor | A router heard on a shared OSPF link. |
| Adjacency | An OSPF relationship that exchanges the needed link-state information. |
| Area | An OSPF grouping of links; connected neighbors must agree on it. |
| Router ID | A 32-bit identifier for a router in OSPF, separate from its local process number. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Discover compatible neighbors.** Check area, addresses where required, timers, authentication and network type.
2. **Exchange the map.** Read neighbor states; stalled database exchange can reflect mismatched maximum packet size, called MTU.
3. **Calculate routes.** Use OSPF costs. Broadcast networks elect a DR and BDR to coordinate exchanges; point-to-point networks do not.

**How to read this:** This is a simplified OSPF workflow. Two ordinary broadcast-segment routers can correctly remain 2-Way with each other while being Full with the elected DR/BDR.

**Keep this in mind:** OSPF process numbers are local; neighboring router IDs should be unique.

<a id="topic-3-4-a"></a>

#### 3.4.a — Forming and verifying neighbors

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.a)

**Start here:** Check the settings neighbors must agree on, then read how far their database exchange has progressed.

Check compatible area, addressing where required, timers, authentication and network type. Router IDs must be unique. Read neighbor state: persistent ExStart/Exchange can indicate MTU problems, while two DROthers can legitimately be 2-Way with each other.

<a id="topic-3-4-b"></a>

#### 3.4.b — OSPF on a point-to-point link

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.b)

**Start here:** Point-to-point OSPF uses no DR/BDR election. Merely setting a /30 address does not select that network type.

A point-to-point network type has no DR/BDR election and supports a full adjacency between its two routers. Configure the intended network type consistently and verify it in interface output. A /30 mask alone does not automatically select OSPF point-to-point behavior on Ethernet.

<a id="topic-3-4-c"></a>

#### 3.4.c — Broadcast segments and DR/BDR elections

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.c)

**Start here:** Broadcast segments choose a DR and BDR by priority then router ID. A later higher-priority router does not immediately replace an existing DR.

On a broadcast network, eligible routers compare interface priority and then router ID. Priority zero excludes an interface from election. An established election is nonpreemptive; a later higher-priority router does not automatically replace the existing DR.

<a id="topic-3-4-d"></a>

#### 3.4.d — OSPF router identity

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.d)

**Start here:** Use a unique router ID. Without an explicit ID, eligible loopback addresses are preferred before physical-interface addresses at selection time.

Prefer an explicit router-id. Otherwise selection normally uses the highest eligible loopback IPv4 address, then the highest eligible nonloopback address at selection time. A router ID is a 32-bit identifier; the local OSPF process number is a different value and need not match neighbors.

#### Objective overview

- Neighbors need compatible area, subnet where required, timers, authentication and network type. MTU problems can prevent database exchange. Router IDs uniquely identify routers; an explicitly configured router ID is predictable.
- On broadcast networks, DR and BDR elections reduce adjacency overhead. Higher interface priority wins, then higher router ID. Priority 0 is ineligible; election is not preemptive. Point-to-point networks need no DR/BDR.
- OSPF cost is based on reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, with a minimum cost of 1. Configure reference bandwidth consistently. Use passive-interface to advertise a connected network without sending hellos there.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 21, 22, 23, 24](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Interpret adjacency state

**Start here:** Neighbor states describe progress toward exchanging the map. On a broadcast segment, ordinary routers need not fully synchronize directly with every other ordinary router because elected coordinators handle that relationship.

A typical progression is Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full. Two DROthers on a broadcast network can normally remain 2-Way with each other and Full with DR/BDR. Persistent ExStart/Exchange calls for checks including MTU and network-type compatibility.

##### Know what configuration selects

**Start here:** The OSPF process number names a local configuration. A network statement selects matching local interfaces and their area; it is not a request to advertise any arbitrary remote network.

The process ID is local and need not match neighbors. network statements select local interfaces by address/wildcard and assign an area; ip ospf 1 area 0 is an interface-based alternative. Router ID selection prefers explicit configuration, then highest eligible loopback IPv4, then nonloopback IPv4 at selection time. OSPFv2 uses IP protocol 89, not TCP port 89.

##### Worked review check

Must neighbors using OSPF process 1 and 10 change those numbers to match?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. The OSPF process number names each router's local configuration. Neighbors instead need compatible link operation, area, addressing where required, timers and other adjacency settings. Their router IDs should also be unique.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Form and verify a single-area OSPFv2 adjacency.

**Covered features:** Neighbors; Router ID; Point-to-point; Broadcast DR/BDR; Cost/passive interfaces.

##### Configure R1; mirror on R2 with its own addresses

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Give R2 different local addresses and identity while matching area, link type and reference bandwidth.

R2 uses 10.0.12.2/30 and a distinct router ID 2.2.2.2. Configure point-to-point and the reference bandwidth consistently. Advertise additional LANs with matching network statements; leave their interfaces passive.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
 no shutdown
exit
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
 passive-interface default
 no passive-interface GigabitEthernet1
 network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
end
```


##### Alternative broadcast-segment election controls

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Study broadcast-segment election separately from the point-to-point example.

This controls eligibility on a broadcast segment; it is not used on the point-to-point link above. A priority of 0 makes a router ineligible. Existing DR/BDR elections are nonpreemptive.

```text
! On a separate broadcast-network lab interface:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip ospf network broadcast
 ip ospf priority 100
end
```


##### Verify adjacency and routes

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Read neighbor state according to the segment type before treating 2-Way as a fault.

On the point-to-point link expect FULL/-. On broadcast links, some DROTHER neighbors remain 2-WAY with each other as part of normal operation.

```text
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf interface brief
show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet1
show ip protocols
show ip route ospf
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Check subnet, area, timers, authentication, MTU, network type and passive status on both ends.
- Changing a router ID may require restarting the OSPF process; that interrupts adjacencies and is not needed for this initial configuration.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The network statement selects matching local interfaces and assigns area 0. passive-interface keeps advertising that connected network without sending OSPF discovery messages on that interface.

```text
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 passive-interface g0/1
! show ip ospf neighbor
! show ip route ospf
```


#### Check your understanding

On a broadcast OSPF segment, which router is preferred as DR?

- **A.** Lowest router ID always
- **B.** Highest priority, then highest router ID
- **C.** Lowest interface IP always
- **D.** Newest neighbor

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Highest priority, then highest router ID**

At a broadcast-segment election, eligible routers compare interface priority first and router ID second, preferring higher values. Priority 0 is ineligible. A later better candidate does not automatically replace an already elected DR.

</details>

Next objective: [3.5 First-hop redundancy concepts](#objective-3-5)

<a id="objective-3-5"></a>

### 3.5 — First-hop redundancy concepts

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.5/commands)

Hosts normally configure one default gateway. FHRPs preserve a stable virtual gateway while the physical forwarding router can change.

#### In everyday language

First-hop redundancy gives computers one stable gateway identity that more than one physical router can provide.

**A familiar example:** A help desk can keep one phone number while a different staff member answers after a shift change.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Virtual gateway | The shared IP and MAC identity clients use as their gateway. |
| Active router | The router currently forwarding for the shared identity in HSRP. |
| Standby router | The router ready to take over in HSRP. |
| Tracking | A configured way to change gateway preference when a monitored condition fails. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Client uses the shared identity.** Its default gateway is the virtual address, not an individual router’s real address.
2. **One router forwards.** The active router serves that identity while the standby is ready.
3. **Role can move.** On a detected failure, another router takes over. Upstream failures need suitable routing and tracking design.

**How to read this:** This illustrates HSRP-style active/standby operation. Other first-hop protocols have different roles and load-sharing behavior.

**Keep this in mind:** Keeping the gateway available does not by itself keep the entire route to a server healthy.

#### Build your understanding

- HSRP uses an active router and a standby router. VRRP uses a master (called active in newer terminology) and backups. They provide a shared virtual IP and MAC to clients.
- If the active gateway fails, another router takes over the virtual identity. The client need not change its configured gateway or know which physical router is forwarding.
- Priority influences the active router; preemption allows a higher-priority router to take over where supported and configured. Interface tracking can reduce priority when an upstream link fails. FHRP does not replace a routing protocol.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 16](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Follow the virtual identity

**Start here:** Clients keep using a virtual address while a different physical router can take over its role. Preemption governs whether a recovered preferred router takes the role back.

A client resolves the virtual gateway IP to a virtual MAC. HSRP changes which router forwards for that identity. Preemption controls whether a recovered higher-priority router retakes the role. Tracking can reduce priority after an upstream failure while the client-facing link remains up.

##### Compare protocol families

**Start here:** HSRP, VRRP and GLBP implement gateway resilience with different role or sharing behavior. All still need healthy routes beyond that first gateway.

VRRP elects an active/master role and backups. GLBP can give different virtual MACs to clients for load sharing. FHRP protects the first hop; it does not replace resilient routing and upstream connectivity. Conceptual comparison is useful even when full deployment is outside the blueprint verb.

##### Worked review check

Why can clients be blackholed after only the active gateway’s upstream fails?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

The router may still hold the active virtual-gateway role because its client-facing link remains healthy. Without suitable tracking and upstream routing/failure detection, it can accept clients' traffic and have nowhere useful to send it. Gateway-role availability is only the first hop.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Provide a virtual first-hop gateway using HSRP.

**Covered features:** FHRP purpose; Virtual IP/MAC; Active/standby; Priority/preemption.

##### Configure R1 as the preferred gateway

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Configure both routers to share the virtual gateway while keeping their real addresses unique.

Configure R2 on the same LAN as .3 with the same virtual .1 and group 10, priority 100, and preempt. Clients use the virtual .1, not a physical router address.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.10.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 10 ip 10.10.10.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Inspect active/standby state

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Verify the active/standby roles and use a controlled lab failure to observe takeover.

HSRP support depends on platform and license. Verify one active and one standby, and test a controlled failure in a disposable lab.

```text
show standby brief
show standby GigabitEthernet1
show ip arp
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A shared virtual gateway does not supply upstream routes or fix a failed Internet path.
- Preemption and interface tracking affect failover; choose tracking rules according to the topology.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** 10.10.10.1 is the client’s stable virtual gateway. .2 and .3 identify the two physical routers; clients do not need to switch their configured gateway between them.

```text
Client default gateway: 10.10.10.1 (virtual)
Router A: 10.10.10.2 → active
Router B: 10.10.10.3 → standby
Failure of A → B assumes virtual gateway.
```


#### Check your understanding

What address should clients normally use with an FHRP?

- **A.** The standby physical address
- **B.** The virtual gateway IP
- **C.** The multicast group IP
- **D.** The router ID

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. The virtual gateway IP**

Clients use the shared virtual gateway IP. The physical router serving that identity can change after a detected failure, so clients do not need to replace their gateway setting with the other router's real address.

</details>

### 4.1 — Inside-source NAT: static mappings and pools

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.1) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.1/commands)

NAT rewrites addresses at a boundary. Inside local identifies the inside host as seen internally; inside global is its translated identity outside.

#### In everyday language

NAT changes address information as traffic crosses a boundary. It is a translation function, separate from security filtering.

**A familiar example:** A receptionist can give callers a public contact number representing an internal extension.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Inside local | The internal address used by the inside device. |
| Inside global | The translated address representing it outside. |
| Pool | A set of addresses available for dynamic translation. |
| PAT/overload | Translation that uses port information so several sessions can share an external address. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Choose the translation model.** Static uses a fixed one-to-one mapping; dynamic draws from a pool.
2. **Identify the boundary and traffic.** Mark inside/outside interfaces and select which sources are translated.
3. **Verify active mappings.** Generate test traffic, inspect translations and check return routing. A full pool can prevent new one-to-one mappings.

**How to read this:** The steps describe translation. An ACL used to select NAT traffic is not automatically an interface security filter.

**Keep this in mind:** For ten dynamic addresses without overload, an eleventh simultaneous inside mapping may have no free address.

#### Build your understanding

- Static NAT creates a fixed one-to-one mapping. Dynamic NAT assigns a mapping from a pool while translations are in use; pool exhaustion can prevent new mappings.
- Mark inside and outside interfaces and define which inside sources are eligible. A NAT classification ACL selects traffic for translation; it is not automatically a security filter.
- PAT (overload) allows many inside sessions to share a global address by tracking transport ports. Verify translations, interface roles, routing, and the classification ACL together.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 14](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read local and global correctly

**Start here:** Local/global describe viewpoints of the same inside host. Without port sharing, a dynamic pool needs one free external mapping address for each active translated inside address.

Inside local describes the inside host internally; inside global describes its translated external identity. A dynamic pool without overload needs an available global address for each simultaneously translated inside address. PAT distinguishes flows sharing a global address using transport information.

##### Validate both directions

**Start here:** Generate traffic from an actual inside client, then check mappings and return routing. A NAT-selection deny means not selected for that translation, not necessarily blocked by a security rule.

Inspect inside/outside roles, classification, translations created by real test traffic and return routing. A NAT ACL selects translation; denying translation does not automatically drop a packet. Clearing stale translations can affect active sessions and needs appropriate lab scope.

##### Worked review check

A dynamic pool has ten global addresses without overload. Why might an eleventh active host fail?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Without overload, each active translated inside address uses one free global address. Ten pool addresses may therefore leave no mapping for the eleventh simultaneous host. Check actual use, then choose sufficient pool space or a suitable PAT design.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Translate private addresses on a NAT-capable router.

**Covered features:** Static NAT; Dynamic NAT pool; PAT overload; Inside local/global.

##### Mark inside/outside and create a static mapping

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Mark the boundary and ensure the outside network can return traffic to the translated address.

The upstream network must deliver the translated address to this router. Documentation addresses represent a closed lab, not real public Internet allocation.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
 no shutdown
exit
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
 no shutdown
exit
ip nat inside source static 10.0.0.10 203.0.113.10
end
```


##### Alternative: dynamic pool or PAT — choose one for the test sources

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Choose either the dynamic pool or port-sharing example for the same test sources.

Do not leave competing source rules active for this same demonstration. PAT shares the outside interface address using session port information.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list standard NAT-SOURCES
 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
exit
! Dynamic one-to-one pool example:
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES pool PUBLIC
end
! PAT alternative: remove the preceding dynamic rule first.
configure terminal
no ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES pool PUBLIC
ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES interface GigabitEthernet2 overload
end
```


##### Generate client traffic, then inspect translations

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Create matching client traffic before expecting dynamic translations to appear.

Dynamic translations appear after matching inside-host traffic. A router-originated ping may not exercise the same inside-to-outside NAT path.

```text
show ip nat translations
show ip nat statistics
show ip access-lists NAT-SOURCES
show ip route
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- NAT is not available on every Catalyst switch; use the labeled router platform.
- A NAT classification ACL selects translations; it is not automatically an interface security filter.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The static mapping pairs 10.0.0.10 with 203.0.113.10. The later pool is a separate dynamic example; its ACL selects sources for translation rather than defining complete access security.

```text
interface g0/0
 ip nat inside
interface g0/1
 ip nat outside
ip nat inside source static 10.0.0.10 203.0.113.10
! Dynamic pool:
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
access-list 1 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC
! show ip nat translations
```


#### Check your understanding

Which NAT type creates a fixed one-to-one address mapping?

- **A.** Static NAT
- **B.** DHCP
- **C.** DNS caching
- **D.** OSPF

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. Static NAT**

Static NAT pairs one chosen internal address with one fixed translated address. Unlike a dynamic pool assignment, the mapping is configured explicitly and does not wait to choose a free address from a pool.

</details>

Next objective: [4.2 NTP clients and servers](#objective-4-2)

<a id="objective-4-2"></a>

### 4.2 — NTP clients and servers

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.2) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.2/commands)

NTP synchronizes device clocks, which is essential for meaningful logs, certificate checks and incident analysis.

#### In everyday language

NTP lets devices adjust their clocks to a selected time source. Matching clocks make event records easier to compare.

**A familiar example:** If two security cameras disagree about time, their recordings can make the same incident look like two different events.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Time server | A device providing time to clients. |
| Stratum | The number of synchronization steps from a reference clock. |
| Offset | The measured difference between clocks. |
| Synchronized | The device has selected and is following a time source. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Choose a suitable source.** Use an intended, reachable and appropriately protected time server.
2. **Verify actual selection.** Check NTP associations and synchronized status; a saved server address alone is not proof.
3. **Interpret the hierarchy.** A client normally advertises its selected server’s stratum plus one. Stratum 16 means unsynchronized.

**How to read this:** This is a time-checking sequence. A lower stratum is not a guarantee that the reference clock is accurate or trustworthy.

**Keep this in mind:** Devices can agree with one another and still share the same wrong time.

#### Build your understanding

- An NTP client synchronizes to an upstream server, normally over UDP 123. A device can also serve time to downstream clients.
- Stratum describes distance from a reference clock. A reference source is stratum 0; a directly attached server is stratum 1. A lower stratum does not by itself guarantee a trustworthy source.
- Configure reliable reachable sources, secure time distribution according to policy, and verify association state and synchronization. A wrong timezone affects display, while NTP operates on a common time base.
- A synchronized NTP device normally advertises a stratum one greater than the server it selected. A server at stratum 4 therefore places its synchronized downstream client at stratum 5, provided the hierarchy remains within synchronized strata 1 through 15. Stratum 16 is unsynchronized. The hierarchy distance is not a guarantee of source accuracy, security or low network delay.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 13](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read association state

**Start here:** Read which source was selected, whether it is reachable and whether synchronization occurred. Stratum is position in a hierarchy, not a certificate of clock trustworthiness.

Inspect peer selection, reachability, offset and synchronized status. Strata 1–15 describe synchronized hierarchy levels; stratum 16 indicates an unsynchronized condition. An NTP server can itself be an upstream client, and a low stratum is not a trust guarantee.

##### Separate time display from reference

**Start here:** A time zone changes display rather than fixing the clock source. A local lab clock can make every client consistently wrong if it is treated as the reference.

Timezone changes local display, not synchronization. A lab ntp master can distribute a wrong clock consistently if treated as an authoritative source. Match supported authentication and access policy at both endpoints and verify the reference itself.

##### Worked review check

Can devices agree on time and all be wrong?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Yes. Devices following the same inaccurate source can agree with one another and all show the wrong time. Verify the reference source itself; synchronization is agreement with a source, not proof of that source's accuracy.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Synchronize a client and understand server mode.

**Covered features:** NTP client; NTP server; Stratum; Verification.

##### Configure authenticated upstream time

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x or IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Match supported authentication settings at the device and its upstream time server.

The server must support the same key ID, algorithm and secret. Use the parser on your image to confirm accepted key encoding; do not use legacy MD5 to work around a current-release restriction.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ntp authenticate
ntp authentication-key 10 hmac-sha2-256 <SHARED_NTP_KEY>
ntp trusted-key 10
ntp server 192.0.2.123 key 10
end
```


##### Dedicated isolated-lab time source — optional

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Use the local time-source example only on the separate isolated lab server.

Run only on the separate lab device intended to serve as an unsynchronized local reference. This is not a trustworthy UTC source for a real network; use a suitable upstream reference instead.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ntp master 8
end
```


##### Verify association and synchronization

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x or IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Wait for synchronization and verify the selected source and status.

Allow time for synchronization. Association output identifies the selected peer; matching keys alone do not prove that its clock is correct.

```text
show ntp associations
show ntp status
show clock detail
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Check routing, UDP 123, source addresses and the matching authentication settings.
- Timezone settings alter displayed local time; NTP synchronizes a common time base.

##### Command references

- [Administering the device — IOS XE 26.x](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/switches/lan/catalyst9300/software/release/26-x/configuration_guide/sys_mgmt/b_26x_sys_mgmt_9300_cg/administering_the_device.html)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** ntp server chooses an upstream source. The commented ntp master example is a lab fallback that can distribute an incorrect local clock; show commands check actual synchronization.

```text
ntp server 192.0.2.123
! Lab-only local time source when no upstream exists:
! ntp master 8
show ntp associations
show ntp status
show clock detail
```


#### Check your understanding

Which UDP port does NTP use?

- **A.** 53
- **B.** 67
- **C.** 123
- **D.** 161

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**C. 123**

NTP uses UDP port 123 for time synchronization. This is an application port number, not a physical socket on the device. Synchronization still needs a suitable reachable source.

</details>

Next objective: [4.3 DHCP and DNS roles](#objective-4-3)

<a id="objective-4-3"></a>

### 4.3 — DHCP and DNS roles

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.3/commands)

DHCP supplies host configuration; DNS maps names to records. They solve different problems and can fail independently.

#### In everyday language

DHCP supplies device settings; DNS looks up records such as the address belonging to a website name.

**A familiar example:** DHCP is like being assigned a room and exit instructions. DNS is like looking a person up in a directory.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Lease | A time-limited DHCP assignment. |
| Option | An extra DHCP setting, such as gateway or DNS server. |
| DNS record | A typed directory entry, such as A for IPv4 or AAAA for IPv6. |
| Cache | A stored answer reused for a limited time. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Discover and offer.** The client looks for DHCP service; a server proposes settings.
2. **Request and acknowledge.** The client requests a lease and the server confirms it. An offer alone is not a completed assignment.
3. **Look up names when needed.** DNS returns records; a correct answer still does not prove the application is reachable.

**How to read this:** The first two steps describe a common initial DHCPv4 exchange. DNS is a separate service, not a fifth DHCP message.

**Keep this in mind:** Correct address settings and correct name lookup are separate dependencies.

#### Build your understanding

- IPv4 DHCP commonly follows Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA). Servers use UDP 67 and clients UDP 68. Options include subnet mask, gateway, DNS servers and lease duration.
- DNS A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME aliases names; MX identifies mail service; PTR supports reverse lookup. DNS commonly uses UDP and TCP 53.
- A DHCP relay forwards client requests across a routed boundary. DNS recursion obtains answers on a client’s behalf; cached records remain valid according to their TTL.
- In an initial DHCPv4 lease exchange, DISCOVER looks for service, OFFER proposes configuration, REQUEST selects or requests the lease, and ACK confirms the server's assignment. A proposal is not a completed lease: the client still needs the successful acknowledgment and valid options. A server can reject an unsuitable request with DHCPNAK, leading the client to restart the appropriate acquisition process.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 19, 28](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 5](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Follow a lease beyond DORA

**Start here:** A lease has a lifecycle after initial assignment. Clients renew it and may seek another server; the actual address, gateway, DNS options and expiration all affect operation.

DORA describes a common initial IPv4 lease. During renewal a client can unicast to its server; rebinding can seek another server. Address, mask, gateway, DNS options and lease state all matter. Link-local assignment warrants investigation rather than assuming a valid routed enterprise lease.

##### Separate names from application access

**Start here:** DNS may reuse a cached answer until its time-to-live expires. That timer is separate from IP packet lifetime; a name answer still does not prove the application connection works.

A resolver may answer from cache until TTL expiry or obtain an answer from other servers. A/AAAA resolution does not prove that an application transport is reachable. PTR reverse lookup is separate from forward name-to-address resolution.

##### Worked review check

A hostname resolves but HTTPS times out. Is changing DNS necessarily the next step?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. First verify that DNS returned the intended address, then inspect the network route, filtering rules, transport connection and application server. Name lookup and successful HTTPS are separate steps, so a timeout does not automatically call for changing DNS.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Provide a small DHCPv4 scope and device DNS resolution.

**Covered features:** DHCP DORA/options; DNS record roles; Ports; Relay relationship.

##### Provide addresses on a connected router LAN

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Provide addresses and options for a real connected client subnet; this does not create the DNS service.

The DNS server address must represent a real reachable resolver in your lab. The pool sends client options; it does not install a DNS server or create A/AAAA records.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
exit
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.20
ip dhcp pool USERS
 network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.10.10.1
 dns-server 192.0.2.53
 domain-name lab.example
end
```


##### Configure DNS for the router’s own lookups

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Set the router’s own name resolver separately from the DNS options sent to clients.

This resolver setting belongs to the router itself; clients obtain their DNS setting from the DHCP pool or their local configuration.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip domain lookup
ip name-server 192.0.2.53
end
```


##### Verify leases and the DNS service path

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Check address leases and name lookups as two independent services.

A DHCP binding does not prove DNS works. A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/PTR records are managed on the DNS service, not by a generic IOS switch command.

```text
show ip dhcp pool
show ip dhcp binding
show ip dhcp conflict
show hosts
ping example.com
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Pool exhaustion, a wrong mask and an incorrect gateway/DNS option produce different symptoms.
- If the server is on another subnet, configure the relay in lesson 4.6.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** DORA abbreviates Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The DNS arrow means the name has an IPv4 A record, not that the web service has already answered.

```text
Client DHCP: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
DNS: www.example.com → A 192.0.2.80
A valid lease can still contain the wrong DNS server or gateway.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which DNS record stores an IPv6 address?

- **A.** A
- **B.** MX
- **C.** AAAA
- **D.** PTR

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**C. AAAA**

An AAAA record stores an IPv6 address for a name. An A record stores an IPv4 address. DNS has separate record types because a name can have different kinds of information.

</details>

Next objective: [4.4 SNMP in network operations](#objective-4-4)

<a id="objective-4-4"></a>

### 4.4 — SNMP in network operations

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.4/commands)

SNMP lets management stations read and sometimes change device information organized in a MIB.

#### In everyday language

SNMP lets a monitoring system ask a device for information such as traffic counts and errors.

**A familiar example:** A supervisor can read a machine’s dashboard without needing permission to change every machine setting.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Manager | The monitoring system asking questions. |
| Agent | The device process answering management requests. |
| OID | An identifier for one managed value. |
| authPriv | An SNMPv3 level providing message authentication and encrypted content. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Ask for a value.** The manager queries an object exposed by the device agent.
2. **Read or notify.** Polling retrieves values; traps send unacknowledged events and informs request acknowledgment.
3. **Limit access.** Use suitable SNMPv3 protection and only the needed read/write permissions.

**How to read this:** These are monitoring roles and safeguards. Authentication checks the message; privacy encrypts its content. They are different protections.

**Keep this in mind:** Read-only monitoring usually does not need configuration-writing permission.

#### Build your understanding

- An SNMP manager queries an agent on a network device. OIDs identify managed objects such as interface counters. Polling obtains values; traps and informs send event notifications.
- Agents commonly listen on UDP 161; notifications commonly use UDP 162. Traps are unacknowledged; informs request acknowledgment.
- SNMPv1/v2c use community strings without modern transport protection. SNMPv3 can provide authentication and privacy (authPriv); authorize only the required views and restrict management sources.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 17](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Compare polling and notifications

**Start here:** A monitor can ask for values, change permitted values or receive events. A notification about one event is not a complete history of all counters.

Get/GetNext/GetBulk retrieve managed values; Set changes writable objects. OIDs identify objects in the MIB. Traps lack acknowledgments while informs request them. Notifications complement polling rather than automatically forming a complete counter history.

##### Apply the actual protection level

**Start here:** SNMPv3 can authenticate without encrypting, or provide both. Give a monitoring account only the objects and read/write permissions it needs.

SNMPv3 noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv provide different protection. Authentication does not imply encryption. Restrict manager sources, permitted views and write capability. Community-based v1/v2c is useful to recognize in older material; current secure designs need appropriate v3 protection.

##### Worked review check

Does authNoPriv hide monitored counters from traffic observers?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. authNoPriv authenticates messages without encrypting their content. Properly configured authPriv adds payload privacy. Reading auth as if it also meant encryption would combine two separate protections.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Configure authenticated and encrypted SNMPv3 polling.

**Covered features:** Manager/agent/MIB; Polling/traps/informs; SNMPv3 authPriv.

##### Restrict the manager and create an authPriv user

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Create matching protected manager credentials and a limited read view.

Replace both secrets and configure matching settings on the NMS. The read-only view covers the MIB in this learning example; narrow it for the intended monitoring task. SHA-2 support must be present on the selected image.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list standard SNMP-MANAGERS
 permit host 192.0.2.50
exit
snmp-server view STUDY iso included
snmp-server group NMS v3 priv read STUDY access SNMP-MANAGERS
snmp-server user monitor NMS v3 auth sha-2 256 <AUTH_SECRET> priv aes 128 <PRIVACY_SECRET>
end
```


##### Inspect group, user and agent counters

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Inspect the SNMP user/group and counters; the manager is the side that asks for values.

SNMP users may not appear as plaintext entries in show running-config; inspect show snmp user. The management station initiates polling to UDP 161.

```text
show snmp user
show snmp group
show snmp
show ip access-lists SNMP-MANAGERS
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A user with authNoPriv is not equivalent to the group’s required authPriv level.
- Configure notifications separately if required; traps use UDP 162 and informs request acknowledgments. SNMPv1/v2c community examples are legacy on current XE.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS SNMP command reference](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/ios-xml/ios/snmp/command/nm-snmp-cr-book/nm-snmp-cr-s5.html)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The protection names build from no authentication/no privacy to authentication only, then both. The arrows compare levels, not a required sequence of configuration steps.

```text
Monitor: interface octets, errors, CPU and memory.
SNMPv3 levels: noAuthNoPriv → authNoPriv → authPriv
Choose authPriv when authentication and encryption are required.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which SNMPv3 level includes authentication and encryption?

- **A.** public
- **B.** noAuthNoPriv
- **C.** authNoPriv
- **D.** authPriv

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**D. authPriv**

In authPriv, auth means messages are authenticated and Priv means their content has privacy through encryption. authNoPriv supplies authentication without that encrypted-content protection.

</details>

Next objective: [4.5 Syslog facilities and severity](#objective-4-5)

<a id="objective-4-5"></a>

### 4.5 — Syslog facilities and severity

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.5/commands)

Syslog centralizes event messages so operators can correlate activity across devices.

#### In everyday language

Syslog records device events. Severity numbers indicate urgency, with smaller numbers meaning more serious events.

**A familiar example:** A collector is a shared incident notebook; matching timestamps help you place related events in order.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Severity | The seriousness level, numbered 0 through 7. |
| Facility | The subsystem or category producing a message. |
| Threshold | The least serious level included at a logging destination. |
| Collector | A server receiving logs from devices. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Read the message.** Identify its source category, numeric severity and event label.
2. **Apply the threshold.** Warnings is level 4, so it includes levels 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
3. **Compare timestamps.** Use synchronized clocks and understand time zones before inferring event order.

**How to read this:** This is a log-reading sequence. Each destination, such as a local buffer or remote collector, can have its own logging settings.

**Keep this in mind:** Level 0 is most urgent; level 7 is debugging.

#### Build your understanding

- Severity runs from 0 (emergency) through 7 (debugging): emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notification, informational, debugging. Lower numbers indicate more serious conditions.
- A logging threshold includes that level and all numerically lower levels. A trap level of warnings (4) sends severities 0–4, not 5–7.
- Facilities categorize message sources. Use timestamps and synchronized clocks. Traditional syslog often uses UDP 514; transport and security options depend on the platform.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 13](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read the message and destination

**Start here:** A Cisco message label identifies a subsystem, seriousness number and event shorthand. A message category is different from the address of its collector.

Cisco messages commonly use %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC. Console, buffered, remote and terminal-monitor logging are distinct destinations. A message facility/mnemonic and a remote syslog facility setting are not the numeric severity.

##### Apply numerical thresholds

**Start here:** Thresholds include their level and every more serious, lower-numbered level. Debug output can be expensive, so collect a narrow sample and stop it when finished.

Levels are 0 emergency, 1 alert, 2 critical, 3 error, 4 warning, 5 notification, 6 informational and 7 debugging. A threshold includes its number and lower numbers. Debugging can be expensive; scope it narrowly and stop after collecting the required evidence.

##### Worked review check

Which severities does logging trap notifications send?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Notifications is severity 5. A remote threshold at that level includes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. It excludes informational 6 and debugging 7; other local or remote logging destinations can use different thresholds.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Send timestamped syslog at a chosen severity threshold.

**Covered features:** Facilities; Severity 0–7; Threshold; Buffered/remote logging.

##### Configure buffered and remote lab logging

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Set local and remote logging separately and note their different included severities.

The remote threshold sends severity 0–4; local buffered informational includes 0–6. Plain UDP syslog is unencrypted in this closed-lab example. Use the platform’s supported authenticated TLS logging design for production.

```text
enable
configure terminal
service timestamps log datetime msec
logging buffered 32768 informational
logging host 192.0.2.50
logging trap warnings
logging facility local7
end
```


##### Inspect timestamps, destinations and messages

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Check the destination, timestamp and collector rules when expected events do not appear.

Check destination reachability and collector filters. A threshold of warnings excludes notifications/informational/debugging messages.

```text
show logging
show clock detail
show running-config | include logging|service timestamps
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Synchronize time before comparing events from multiple devices.
- A facility is a category, not a severity level.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** logging trap warnings sends 0–4 to the remote destination. It excludes notification 5, informational 6 and debugging 7; trap here names the logging threshold, not an SNMP trap.

```text
service timestamps log datetime msec
logging host 192.0.2.50
logging trap warnings
show logging
! Sent: emergency, alert, critical, error, warning
```


#### Check your understanding

With logging trap warnings, which severity is included?

- **A.** Debugging (7)
- **B.** Informational (6)
- **C.** Notification (5)
- **D.** Error (3)

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**D. Error (3)**

Warnings is severity 4. The threshold includes its own level and all more serious lower numbers: 0 through 4. Error is 3, so it is included; informational 6 and debugging 7 are not.

</details>

Next objective: [4.6 DHCP clients and relays](#objective-4-6)

<a id="objective-4-6"></a>

### 4.6 — DHCP clients and relays

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.6) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.6/commands)

Routers can obtain an address through DHCP and relay requests for clients on other subnets.

#### In everyday language

A DHCP relay carries local clients’ address requests to a server on another network. A DHCP client asks for its own settings.

**A familiar example:** A receptionist forwarding someone else’s form has a different job from a person filling in their own form.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Client | The device requesting its own address settings. |
| Relay | A gateway forwarding client DHCP messages to a server. |
| Server pool | Settings and available addresses for a particular subnet. |
| giaddr | The relay-address field helping the server identify the client subnet. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Receive a local request.** The client broadcasts on its own subnet.
2. **Relay from the gateway.** The client-facing routed interface forwards the request to the configured server and identifies the subnet.
3. **Return suitable settings.** The server selects the correct pool and replies over a working return path.

**How to read this:** This describes relaying across a routed boundary. A helper on the client’s Layer 3 gateway is different from an endpoint access-port assignment.

**Keep this in mind:** ip address dhcp requests settings; ip helper-address forwards other clients’ requests.

#### Build your understanding

- A router interface can use ip address dhcp as a DHCP client. For downstream hosts, ip helper-address belongs on the interface receiving their broadcasts.
- The relay sets gateway information (giaddr) so the DHCP server can choose the correct subnet pool. The server needs a return route and a correctly scoped pool.
- Check VLAN, relay interface, helper address, pool exhaustion, exclusions, and reachability. IOS helper behavior may also forward other UDP services; restrict according to policy.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 6, 19](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Trace a relayed request

**Start here:** The gateway relays a local request and identifies the client subnet so the remote server chooses the right address pool. The server must also be able to send its reply back.

A client broadcasts locally. A relay on the client-facing routed interface forwards to the server and supplies gateway information so the server selects a pool. The server needs a usable return path and a correctly scoped pool.

##### Keep client, relay and server distinct

**Start here:** A device can request its own address or relay someone else’s request. Neither role alone creates a DHCP server or an appropriate remote client pool.

ip address dhcp makes an interface a DHCP client; ip helper-address supplies relay behavior. Neither automatically configures a DHCP server. A Layer 2 switch management client may still need an appropriate default gateway for remote reachability.

##### Worked review check

Does a VLAN 20 access port normally receive the helper-address command?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. The helper belongs on VLAN 20's Layer 3 gateway interface or SVI. That is the point receiving local client broadcasts and forwarding them to the remote server with the client-subnet context. An ordinary access port only places its host into the VLAN.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Configure a DHCP client and relay broadcasts to a remote server.

**Covered features:** IOS DHCP client; DHCP relay; giaddr; Verification.

##### Get the WAN address from DHCP

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Make this router interface request its own settings from the upstream lab server.

Use this on an interface connected to a lab DHCP server. It is an alternative to the static outside-address example in lesson 4.1.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip address dhcp
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Relay a client subnet to a remote server

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Relay on the client’s gateway interface and provide a suitable remote pool and return route.

Place the helper on the client-facing Layer 3 interface. The remote server needs a pool for 10.20.20.0/24 and return reachability to the relay. No helper is needed if the server directly shares the client VLAN.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.20.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 192.0.2.10
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Verify client interface, relay and routes

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Check the client interface, relay and remote server rather than relying only on the router’s local lease list.

Local show ip dhcp binding reports leases served by this IOS device, not every lease on a remote DHCP server. Check the remote server as well.

```text
show dhcp lease
show ip interface brief
show running-config interface GigabitEthernet1
show ip route 192.0.2.10
ping 192.0.2.10
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Check the client VLAN and DHCP snooping trust before changing the helper address.
- ip helper-address can forward additional UDP services depending on platform defaults; review the intended forwarding policy.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** g0/0 is shown as a DHCP client. g0/1 is a separate relay-facing example with its own static gateway address and helper pointing to the DHCP server.

```text
interface g0/0
 ip address dhcp
interface g0/1
 ip address 10.20.0.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 192.0.2.10
! Client VLAN 20 requests are relayed to 192.0.2.10.
```


#### Check your understanding

Where is ip helper-address configured for a client subnet?

- **A.** The client-facing Layer 3 interface
- **B.** Every access port
- **C.** Only the DNS server
- **D.** The console line

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. The client-facing Layer 3 interface**

Put the helper on the routed gateway interface receiving the clients' local DHCP broadcasts. That interface can forward the request to the remote server and identify the client subnet. An ordinary Layer 2 access port does not perform that relay job.

</details>

Next objective: [4.7 QoS per-hop forwarding behavior](#objective-4-7)

<a id="objective-4-7"></a>

### 4.7 — QoS per-hop forwarding behavior

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.7) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.7/commands)

QoS manages contention. It cannot create bandwidth, but it can prioritize delay-sensitive traffic and control congestion.

#### In everyday language

QoS decides how shared network capacity is used when traffic competes. It cannot create extra cable capacity.

**A familiar example:** A queue can let urgent customers go first or ask a busy customer to wait, but it cannot make a single cashier serve infinitely fast.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Classification | Deciding which traffic group a packet belongs to. |
| Marking | Writing a label so other devices can recognize its intended treatment. |
| Policing | Dropping or relabeling traffic exceeding a configured rate. |
| Shaping | Holding traffic in a queue and sending it later to smooth the rate. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Identify and label.** Classify traffic and apply intended markings such as DSCP.
2. **Choose who waits.** Schedule queues so delay-sensitive traffic gets suitable treatment without starving everything else.
3. **Control excess.** Police by dropping/remarking, or shape by buffering. Buffered packets wait longer.

**How to read this:** This compares traffic treatment. A label requests a policy behavior; each downstream device must implement the intended policy.

**Keep this in mind:** Shaping trades extra waiting for a smoother sending rate.

#### Build your understanding

- Classification identifies traffic; marking labels it, commonly using IP DSCP or Layer 2 CoS. Trust markings only at an intentional boundary.
- Queuing schedules packets during congestion. Low-latency priority queuing supports voice, but must be bounded to prevent starving other traffic. Congestion avoidance can drop selected traffic before a queue is full.
- Policing enforces a rate by dropping or remarking excess traffic. Shaping buffers traffic to smooth bursts toward a configured rate, adding delay. Per-hop behavior describes how each router treats a marked class.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 15](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Keep markings distinct

**Start here:** Labels at different layers have different sizes: DSCP uses six IP-header bits and CoS/PCP uses three VLAN-tag bits. A policy can translate between labels without making them the same field.

DSCP is a six-bit IP marking; CoS/PCP is three bits in an 802.1Q tag. EF commonly uses DSCP 46, with AF/class-selector values for other behaviors. CoS 5 is not the same encoded field as DSCP 46, although a policy can map them.

##### Understand congestion behavior

**Start here:** Delay is waiting/travel time; jitter is variation in that time; loss means missing packets. Priority scheduling, early drops, policing and shaping affect these in different ways.

Delay is transit time, jitter is delay variation, and loss is missing traffic. Bounded priority scheduling manages contention. Policing drops/remarks excess traffic; shaping buffers it for later transmission. Congestion avoidance can drop selectively before queues fill to influence responsive flows.

##### Worked review check

Why can shaping meet a WAN rate while increasing voice delay?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Shaping makes excess packets wait before sending them, so a smoother rate can add delay. Choose the rate, burst behavior and queue/priority design so the waiting time still suits the intended application, especially voice.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Classify, mark, queue, police and shape on a supported router.

**Covered features:** Classification/marking; Queuing; Congestion avoidance; Policing; Shaping.

##### Classify and mark a lab application

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Identify the intended lab application and label only traffic you have reason to trust.

The UDP range is a lab classification example, not a universal detector of voice. Mark only trusted/verified traffic and apply supported policies to appropriate interfaces.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list extended VOICE-SOURCES
 permit udp 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 any range 16384 32767
exit
class-map match-any LAB-VOICE
 match access-group name VOICE-SOURCES
exit
policy-map MARK-LAB
 class LAB-VOICE
  set dscp ef
exit
exit
interface GigabitEthernet1
 service-policy input MARK-LAB
end
```


##### Demonstrate an egress priority queue

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Give bounded priority treatment on a platform supporting the shown queue design.

This illustrates software-router MQC. Catalyst ASIC QoS has platform-specific queues and restrictions; do not assume the same policy is supported on a switch.

```text
enable
configure terminal
class-map match-any EF-TRAFFIC
 match dscp ef
exit
policy-map WAN-QUEUE
 class EF-TRAFFIC
  priority percent 10
 class class-default
  fair-queue
exit
interface GigabitEthernet2
 service-policy output WAN-QUEUE
end
```


##### Alternative rate controls — inspect syntax first

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Choose a shaping alternative deliberately; defining it alone does not attach it.

The shaping policy definition alone does not attach it. Apply an alternative policy deliberately; only one policy of the relevant type/direction is supported on many interfaces. Policing uses police rather than shape and drops/remarks excess instead of buffering.

```text
configure terminal
policy-map LAB-SHAPE
 class class-default
  shape average 10000000
end
! Inspect applied policy counters:
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet2
```


##### Define alternative policing and congestion avoidance policies

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Compare dropping excess traffic with early-drop behavior; check platform support before applying either.

These are separate policy definitions. Policing enforces a 10 Mbps rate by dropping excess traffic; WRED makes early-drop decisions using DSCP thresholds where supported. Definition alone does not apply a policy: attach the chosen policy in a supported direction instead of a conflicting existing policy. Hardware support, queue model and policy compatibility must be checked first.

```text
enable
configure terminal
policy-map LAB-POLICE
 class class-default
  police cir 10000000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
exit
exit
policy-map LAB-WRED
 class class-default
  random-detect dscp-based
end
```


##### Verify live classification and queue counters

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Generate load and watch which queues and rules actually match or drop traffic.

Generate traffic and read matched packets, marks, offered rates and drops. Congestion behavior is meaningful only under load.

```text
show class-map
show policy-map
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet1
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet2
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Bandwidth units, hierarchical support, WRED support and policer syntax vary by forwarding platform.
- Use interface policy counters rather than assuming that a policy definition is active.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The first arrow chain is a processing pipeline. Police and shape are alternatives for excess traffic, not two words for the same action.

```text
Pipeline: classify → mark → queue/schedule → transmit
Police: excess packet → drop or remark
Shape:  excess packet → buffer and send later
```


#### Check your understanding

Which mechanism buffers traffic to smooth it to a configured rate?

- **A.** Policing
- **B.** Shaping
- **C.** ARP
- **D.** NAT

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Shaping**

Shaping holds excess packets in a queue and sends them later at the intended rate. That smooths bursts but can add waiting time. Policing instead normally drops or relabels excess traffic rather than buffering it for later.

</details>

Next objective: [4.8 SSH remote access](#objective-4-8)

<a id="objective-4-8"></a>

### 4.8 — SSH remote access

**Exam target:** Configure.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.8) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.8/commands)

A secure remote CLI requires reachable management addressing, server keys, user authentication and VTY policy.

#### In everyday language

SSH provides an encrypted remote command session, but the network path, device identity and login settings must all work.

**A familiar example:** A locked conversation is useful only if you know you are talking to the intended person.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Host key | The server key used to help verify the device’s identity. |
| VTY lines | The logical remote terminal connections on a Cisco device. |
| Local login | Checking a username and secret in the device’s own account database. |
| Access-class | A rule restricting which sources may use the remote login lines. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Reach and identify the device.** Verify management addressing and the expected host key; investigate changed-key warnings through a trusted channel.
2. **Protect and authenticate.** Enable supported SSH, server keys and the intended user authentication.
3. **Test permitted access.** Check the allowed source path, login and permissions; retain an authorized recovery route.

**How to read this:** This is the SSH access chain. A working encrypted transport does not automatically select local accounts or allow every source subnet.

**Keep this in mind:** transport input ssh selects the transport; login local selects the local user database in the non-AAA example.

#### Build your understanding

- Configure a hostname and domain name, generate an RSA key pair, and enable SSH version 2 where supported. The exact key algorithm options vary by IOS version.
- Create a local user with a secret or configure AAA. VTY lines need login local (or an AAA method) and transport input ssh to accept SSH.
- Use access controls to limit management sources. Verify show ip ssh and test the intended user path; console recovery is useful before changing live remote authentication.
- SSH server host keys help authenticate the device, separately from the user's login. A changed-key warning may follow an authorized device/key replacement, a wrong target or impersonation. Verify the expected device and fingerprint through a trusted independent channel before accepting a new key or sending credentials. Encryption to an unverified peer does not establish that it is the intended router.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 6](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 10](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Verify the access chain

**Start here:** Test the full chain: network path, server keys, SSH settings, user authentication and remote-line policy. One working piece does not create the entire service.

SSH needs operational management addressing, routes, server keys, supported protocol settings, authentication and VTY policy. A password or key alone does not establish a reachable encrypted service. Configure the intended VTY range for the specific platform.

##### Distinguish control locations

**Start here:** A VTY access-class controls sources allowed to log into the device. An interface access-group filters packets on that traffic path; they are different attachment points.
