| Client subnet | The IP address block assigned to that client network. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Set Personal security.** Choose WPA2, AES-CCMP and PSK rather than Enterprise 802.1X.
2. **Map and enable the WLAN.** Attach it to the intended VLAN/policy and AP.
3. **Test beyond the password.** Verify the client’s address, gateway, name lookup and allowed application access.

**How to read this:** These are conceptual steps; controller menus vary. Ordinary ASCII passphrases use 8–63 characters; supported 64-hex raw keys are a different input format.

**Keep this in mind:** A successful password check can coexist with a wrong VLAN or missing DHCP service.

#### Build your understanding

- In the WLC WLAN security page, select WPA2 policy, AES/CCMP encryption and PSK authentication. Enter a strong passphrase and enable the WLAN.
- Map the WLAN to the appropriate policy/interface and VLAN. A correct password cannot compensate for an unavailable VLAN, DHCP server or gateway.
- Validate with a client: association, security negotiation, authentication, address assignment, gateway reachability, DNS and application access. Separate an authentication failure from a post-authentication IP problem.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 4](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Configure the object chain

**Start here:** Build the entire controller relationship: the wireless name/security, its client VLAN policy, the mapping between them and the AP receiving that mapping.

On 9800, create/enable the WLAN profile with SSID, WPA2/AES-CCMP and PSK; create/enable the policy profile for the client VLAN; map them with a policy tag and apply it to the intended AP. AireOS has a different WLAN/dynamic-interface workflow.

##### Validate beyond association

**Start here:** After wireless login, test the assigned network and services. A wrong subnet is a mapping/address-service issue, not automatically a wrong passphrase.

Verify matching PSK, negotiated security, client VLAN, DHCP, gateway, DNS and application access. PSKs commonly use an 8–63-character passphrase or supported 64-hex raw-key format. Match the controller’s selected format rather than pasting a key into an arbitrary field.

##### Worked review check

A client authenticates but gets an address from the wrong subnet. Is retyping its PSK the direct fix?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. Authentication succeeded, while the wrong subnet points to the assigned client network. Trace the AP's policy tag/profile or AireOS interface mapping, then the DHCP service for that VLAN. Retyping a correct password does not repair that mapping.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Create a WPA2-Personal WLAN and connect it to a client VLAN.

**Covered features:** WPA2-PSK/AES; WLAN/policy/tag; AP assignment; Client validation.

##### Create an SSID with AES and a lab PSK

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

**In plain language:** Create the lab WLAN with its intended visible name and replace the sample shared-key placeholder.

Use a new lab WLAN. The SSID is Staff-Lab; STAFF is the profile name. Replace the PSK placeholder; its 0 denotes plaintext input to the command, not a recommendation to keep exposed secrets. Exact secure-secret options depend on the controller release.

```text
enable
configure terminal
wlan STAFF 10 Staff-Lab
 shutdown
 security wpa wpa2
 security wpa wpa2 ciphers aes
 no security wpa akm dot1x
 security wpa psk set-key ascii 0 <REPLACE_WITH_LONG_UNIQUE_PSK>
 security wpa akm psk
 no shutdown
exit
wireless profile policy STAFF-POLICY
 vlan 20
 no shutdown
exit
wireless tag policy LAB-TAG
 wlan STAFF policy STAFF-POLICY
end
```


##### Assign the policy tag to the intended AP

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

**In plain language:** Apply the policy tag using the AP’s own identity, not a wireless client’s MAC.

Replace the sample with the AP Ethernet/base MAC from show ap summary, not a client MAC. The AP must already be joined; management/site/RF settings and the client VLAN/DHCP/routing path must exist. A tag change can cause an AP to rejoin.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ap aaaa.bbbb.cccc
 policy-tag LAB-TAG
end
```


##### Verify every mapping and the client

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

**In plain language:** Inspect one real client’s security, VLAN, IP settings and permitted reachability.

The client MAC is different from the AP MAC. Confirm association/authentication, assigned VLAN 20, IP address and reachability. GUI: Configuration → Tags & Profiles → WLANs / Policy / Tags.

```text
show wlan name STAFF
show wireless profile policy detailed STAFF-POLICY
show wireless tag policy detailed LAB-TAG
show ap tag summary
show wireless client summary
show wireless client mac-address dddd.eeee.ffff detail
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Security fields may need the WLAN shut down while edited; use a maintenance window on an existing service.
- A correct PSK alone cannot fix an absent client VLAN, DHCP service or gateway.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9800 controller configuration guides](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/wireless/catalyst-9800-series-wireless-controllers/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9800 PSK configuration — IOS XE 26.x](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/wireless/controller/9800/26-1/configuration-guide/wl-26-1-cg/private-sk/private-psk.html)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The menu path is illustrative. After Apply, inspect a real client’s security and VLAN/address result rather than treating the saved screen as complete proof.

```text
GUI: WLANs → Staff → Security → Layer 2
Select WPA2 + AES + PSK → enter passphrase → Apply → enable
Then confirm client status and its assigned VLAN/IP.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which combination is appropriate for WPA2-Personal?

- **A.** AES-CCMP and PSK
- **B.** WEP and Telnet
- **C.** Open authentication only
- **D.** TKIP and no password

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. AES-CCMP and PSK**

WPA2-Personal uses a pre-shared key, or PSK, with AES-CCMP data protection. Enterprise 802.1X is a different authentication choice, even when the data-protection cipher is also AES-CCMP.

</details>

Next objective: [6.1 Automation and network management](#objective-6-1)

<a id="domain-6-0"></a>

## 6.0 Automation & Programmability — 10%

Explore controllers, APIs, AI, and infrastructure as code.

7 objectives · 2 lettered subtopics

<a id="objective-6-1"></a>

### 6.1 — Automation and network management

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.1) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.1/commands)

Automation turns repeatable intent into consistent changes, while verification and human judgment still matter.

#### In everyday language

Automation lets software repeat network tasks consistently. It can also repeat a mistake very quickly.

**A familiar example:** A spreadsheet formula saves work across many rows, but a wrong formula copies the same error everywhere.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Intended state | What the approved design says settings should be. |
| Drift | A difference between intended and actual state. |
| Idempotent | Reapplying the same desired state does not create extra unwanted changes. |
| Rollback | A way to restore an earlier working state. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Observe before changing.** Collect current facts and compare them with the approved intended state.
2. **Review and limit the first change.** Inspect the differences and test on a small representative group.
3. **Verify and expand.** Check actual results, keep recovery available, then extend the change.

**How to read this:** This is an automation workflow. A successful command or API response can confirm a request without proving that users can reach their applications.

**Keep this in mind:** Automate verification and recovery planning as well as configuration.

#### Build your understanding

- Templates and scripts reduce repetitive work, configuration drift and inconsistent policy. Inventory, backups, compliance checks and provisioning are common starting points.
- Automation can spread an error quickly. Use version control, validation, staged rollout, idempotent operations and rollback plans. Measure results instead of assuming a successful API response proves the network works.
- A source of truth describes intended state. Comparing intended and actual state helps identify drift; collecting facts should precede changes when the current state is uncertain.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 21, 24](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Compare intent and observation

**Start here:** First compare approved intent with observed settings. A difference needs a decision: repair the live state, update the approved design or investigate before changing anything.

Collect inventory/state, compare it with a versioned source of truth, create a controlled change and verify results. Drift may justify correction, an approved intent update or investigation rather than blindly overwriting actual configuration.

##### Limit the blast radius

**Start here:** Limit how widely a mistake can spread. Review differences, start small and keep recovery ready; a tool reporting success does not prove the user service is healthy.

Use validated templates, limited initial targets, appropriate privileges, reviewable diffs and rollback. Idempotent modules can converge, but arbitrary shell tasks are not automatically idempotent. A successful exit code does not prove end-to-end application health.

##### Worked review check

Why is a successful API response insufficient proof of user reachability?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

An API success can mean a request was accepted or a setting changed. It does not test all dependencies needed by a user. Check the resulting device state and actual application path, including routes, filters and reply traffic.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Use repeatable observations and preserve a reviewed configuration.

**Covered features:** Automation impact; Intended/actual state; Idempotence; Verification.

##### Collect facts before and after a change

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Collect comparable device facts before and after the planned change.

Automation should collect the same facts used during manual troubleshooting. Store snapshots securely and compare intended with observed state; neither a script exit code nor configuration text proves forwarding works.

```text
show version
show interfaces description
show ip interface brief
show vlan brief
show running-config interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
```


##### Persist a validated lab configuration

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Save only after verification; the save command does not create the surrounding automation workflow.

Save only after checking the intended behavior. Automation orchestration, version control, approvals and rollback execution live in the management tooling; the copy command alone does not implement them.

```text
copy running-config startup-config
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Repeated execution should converge toward intended state; avoid blindly appending duplicate lines.
- Configuration backups can contain secrets. Keep them out of shared public repositories.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** Each arrow is a workflow stage. Idempotence means repeating the desired-state operation leaves the intended result stable; arbitrary repeated commands do not automatically have that property.

```text
Workflow: collect facts → validate intent → generate change → review diff → apply → verify → record.
Idempotent: repeating the same intended-state operation does not create extra changes.
```


#### Check your understanding

What does idempotence mean in configuration automation?

- **A.** Every run changes every device
- **B.** Repeated application converges without unnecessary changes
- **C.** Scripts never fail
- **D.** No verification is needed

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Repeated application converges without unnecessary changes**

An idempotent desired-state action leaves the intended state stable when repeated. For example, ensuring a hostname is R1 should not keep making new changes once it is R1. Arbitrary repeated shell commands do not automatically behave this way.

</details>

Next objective: [6.2 Traditional and controller-based networks](#objective-6-2)

<a id="objective-6-2"></a>

### 6.2 — Traditional and controller-based networks

**Exam target:** Compare.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.2) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.2/commands)

Traditional device management configures individual devices; controller-based networking provides a coordinated view and programmable control.

#### In everyday language

A controller coordinates many devices, but those devices still have their own forwarding work and software.

**A familiar example:** A fleet office coordinates buses; it does not replace each bus’s engine or maintenance schedule.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Controller-based | Management or control coordinated through a controller system. |
| Traditional management | Administering devices through their individual interfaces. |
| Forwarding state | The information a device currently uses to deliver traffic. |
| Compatibility | Whether particular controller and device software versions support working together. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Coordinate policy.** Use the controller’s supported inventory, templates and policy workflows.
2. **Keep devices healthy.** Maintain compatible device software as well as controller software.
3. **Plan controller loss.** Check which installed functions continue and which changes/services require the controller.

**How to read this:** These are responsibilities, not a requirement for user packets to pass through the controller. Failure behavior depends on the architecture.

**Keep this in mind:** Centralized management does not remove device software maintenance.

#### Build your understanding

- Each device still forwards traffic, but a controller can centralize policy, inventory, assurance and intent. Centralized management is not the same as forcing all user data through the controller.
- Traditional management commonly uses device-specific CLI or APIs. A controller exposes abstractions for consistent changes across many devices.
- Controller availability, scale, compatibility, security and failure behavior matter. Distributed control can continue some functions during controller failure depending on the design.
- Controller management does not remove the operating system or software lifecycle of each managed network device. Maintain supported device images as well as the controller, verify their compatibility matrix and plan updates for both. An updated controller cannot by itself patch every vulnerability in a switch image; centralized policy and inventory support that maintenance rather than replacing it.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 21, 22](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Separate control and forwarding

**Start here:** A controller can coordinate decisions while switches still forward packets locally. A logically centralized controller system can also be a resilient group of servers.

Traditional devices can run distributed routing and expose local configuration. Controllers centralize abstractions/policy while devices forward packets. Logical centralization may use a resilient cluster; it does not require one physical server.

##### Compare failure behavior

**Start here:** Ask what happens to each function when control connectivity fails. Some forwarding can continue from installed state while policy changes or other services become unavailable.

Controller inventory, templates and assurance coordinate many devices. Compatibility and outage behavior depend on architecture: controller loss neither universally stops all forwarding nor universally leaves every service unaffected. Identify state and functions that remain local.

##### Worked review check

Does a northbound API imply that every user packet traverses the controller?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. A northbound API connects an application with controller functions. User data follows the actual device and tunnel design, which need not pass through the controller. Configuration relationships and packet paths are different diagrams.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Expose management APIs while preserving the forwarding/control distinction.

**Covered features:** Traditional CLI; Controller-based management; Central policy; Data path.

##### Enable NETCONF on a lab management plane

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Enable a supported management API only after authentication and source-access controls are ready.

NETCONF over SSH usually listens on TCP 830. Preconfigure SSH credentials/AAA and restrict management reachability. Enabling an API does not enroll the device into Catalyst Center or move all data through a controller.

```text
enable
configure terminal
netconf-yang
end
```


##### Inspect management services and reachability

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Check management service health independently of traffic forwarding and controller enrollment.

Inspect service health and sessions separately from forwarding. Full controller onboarding is performed using that controller’s supported workflow and credentials.

```text
show platform software yang-management process
show netconf-yang sessions
show ip route
show interfaces status
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- The controller northbound API and the device NETCONF interface are different endpoints.
- Confirm the license, software personality and supported management feature set before enabling a protocol.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The arrows show who configures whom. They do not show the physical path taken by every user packet.

```text
Traditional: operator → device A, then B, then C
Controller-based: operator/API → controller policy → coordinated device configuration
```


#### Check your understanding

What is a key controller-based networking benefit?

- **A.** Removing every data-plane device
- **B.** Centralized policy and coordinated management
- **C.** Eliminating all network failures
- **D.** Replacing IP addressing

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Centralized policy and coordinated management**

A controller can coordinate policy and administration across many devices. Those devices still forward traffic and run software; centralized coordination does not mean every user packet must pass through the controller.

</details>

Next objective: [6.3 Software-defined network architecture](#objective-6-3)

<a id="objective-6-3"></a>

### 6.3 — Software-defined network architecture

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.3/commands)

Software-defined networking separates functions into understandable planes and provides programmable interfaces between them.

#### In everyday language

Networking functions can be separated into deciding paths, forwarding packets and administering the system.

**A familiar example:** A traffic planner decides routes, a junction moves vehicles and an operator changes settings and reads counters.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Control plane | The functions that learn or calculate forwarding information. |
| Data plane | The functions that forward traffic using that information. |
| Management plane | The functions for configuration and observation. |
| Underlay/overlay | The transport network underneath, and logical connectivity built over it. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Applications express intent.** A northbound API commonly connects applications to a controller.
2. **Controller coordinates infrastructure.** A southbound interface commonly connects it to managed devices.
3. **Devices forward traffic.** The data path uses the actual network, including underlay transport and any overlay tunnels.

**How to read this:** North and south are architecture labels, not compass directions. This management/control relationship is distinct from the user-data path.

**Keep this in mind:** An overlay still depends on working connectivity beneath it.

<a id="topic-6-3-a"></a>

#### 6.3.a — Control decisions versus packet forwarding

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.3/6.3.a)

**Start here:** The control plane builds forwarding information; the data plane uses it. Management configures and observes both.

The control plane learns/calculates reachability while the data plane forwards using the resulting information. Management configures and observes these functions. Logical separation does not require every user packet to traverse a central controller.

<a id="topic-6-3-b"></a>

#### 6.3.b — Application-facing and device-facing APIs

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.3/6.3.b)

**Start here:** Applications commonly use the controller’s northbound side; managed infrastructure is on its southbound side. These labels do not describe geographic directions.

Northbound interfaces commonly connect applications to controllers; southbound interfaces connect controller functions to network infrastructure. Distinguish the API direction from the underlay transport and overlay data path, and read the actual architecture rather than assuming one protocol fits all controllers.

#### Objective overview

- The data plane forwards packets. The control plane builds forwarding information. The management plane supports configuration, telemetry and administration.
- An underlay provides IP connectivity; an overlay creates logical connectivity on top using encapsulation. A fabric combines underlay, overlay and control services into an integrated system.
- Northbound APIs connect applications and a controller; southbound APIs connect the controller and network infrastructure. Centralization is logical and need not mean a single physical controller.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 21, 22](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Relate functions and interfaces

**Start here:** Control decides where traffic should go; data forwarding moves it; management observes and configures. Northbound and southbound describe interfaces relative to the controller.

The control plane learns/calculates reachability, the data plane forwards and the management plane configures/observes. Northbound APIs typically connect applications to controllers; southbound interfaces connect controller functions to infrastructure.

##### Use a concrete example

**Start here:** In one Cisco fabric example, the underlay transports packets, VXLAN wraps overlay traffic, and LISP helps locate endpoints. These are an example architecture, not universal SDN requirements.

In SD-Access, underlay IP provides transport, VXLAN supplies overlay data encapsulation and LISP supports endpoint-location/control functions. Catalyst Center coordinates provisioning and assurance. These examples do not imply every SDN system uses the same protocols.

##### Worked review check

Overlay peers cannot reach one another through IP. What dependency comes first?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

First check the underlay: the IP routes, reachability and allowed transport between overlay endpoints. The logical tunnel rides over that network, so its policy cannot compensate for a broken basic path underneath it.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Observe planes and APIs without pretending a fabric is one command.

**Covered features:** Overlay/underlay/fabric; Control/data/management planes; Northbound/southbound APIs.

##### Compare control-plane routes and forwarding state

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Compare learned routes with forwarding and neighbor resolution information.

The routing table describes control-plane decisions; CEF/adjacencies support forwarding. The management interface is used to observe/configure the device. These are related views, not three independently cabled planes.

```text
show ip route
show ip cef
show adjacency
show interfaces description
```


##### Inspect existing tunnel and management services

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

**In plain language:** Inspect existing tunnels and their underlying connectivity; these checks do not create a full fabric.

A configured tunnel can carry overlay traffic while the underlay must reach its endpoint. VXLAN/SD-Access fabrics require specific hardware, control-plane design and controller workflows; this does not create one.

```text
show interfaces Tunnel10
show ip route 198.51.100.2
show netconf-yang sessions
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A Tunnel10 interface is only meaningful if your lab actually configured it.
- Northbound/southbound describes an API relationship, not a fixed TCP port or universal IOS CLI command.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The vertical arrows show application/controller/device interfaces. The final forwarding arrow describes user traffic; it does not require a detour through the application or controller.

```text
Application
   ↕ northbound API
Controller / policy
   ↕ southbound API
Network devices → data-plane forwarding
Overlay tunnels ride on underlay reachability.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which plane performs packet forwarding?

- **A.** Management plane
- **B.** Data plane
- **C.** Accounting plane
- **D.** Application plane

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Data plane**

The data plane is the part that forwards packets using installed forwarding information. The control plane learns or calculates that information, and the management plane supports administration and observation.

</details>

Next objective: [6.4 Generative AI, predictive AI and ML in operations](#objective-6-4)

<a id="objective-6-4"></a>

### 6.4 — Generative AI, predictive AI and ML in operations

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.4/commands)

AI systems can assist network operations through classification, prediction, summarization and pattern detection.

#### In everyday language

AI can summarize information, predict conditions and highlight patterns, but its output needs checking against actual network evidence.

**A familiar example:** A weather forecast helps planning without proving it will rain at one exact location.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Predictive AI | Estimating an outcome, such as future congestion. |
| Generative AI | Producing new content, such as a summary or configuration draft. |
| Telemetry | Measurements collected from devices and services. |
| False positive | An alert that labels normal behavior as a problem. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Supply representative evidence.** Include normal busy periods as well as quiet periods.
2. **Read the output as a proposal.** A prediction or fluent explanation can still be wrong.
3. **Verify before acting.** Check device support, observed state and policy, then use a controlled change.

**How to read this:** The steps show an evidence workflow. A model trained only on quiet nights may misclassify a normal daytime backup.

**Keep this in mind:** The actual device parser and supported documentation take precedence over an unsupported generated command.

#### Build your understanding

- Predictive AI estimates likely events, such as capacity pressure or anomaly likelihood. Generative AI produces content such as explanations, summaries or draft configuration.
- Machine learning finds patterns in data to support anomaly detection, forecasting and event correlation. Useful results depend on representative telemetry and data quality.
- Validate recommendations against actual state and policy. Generated commands can be incorrect; protect sensitive configuration and require appropriate review for impactful changes.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 22](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Match technique to output

**Start here:** Forecasting a future condition is predictive. Writing a new summary or draft is generative. Pattern recognition helps investigate without proving a proposed cause is correct.

Predictive models estimate outcomes such as congestion or anomaly likelihood. Generative models produce explanations or configuration drafts. ML can classify and correlate data; a fluent generated answer is not independent evidence that its proposed cause is correct.

##### Control evidence and action

**Start here:** Compare AI output with representative measurements and the actual device. Wrong baseline data can create false alarms, and plausible commands may be unsupported.

Check representative telemetry, time windows, false positives, sensitivity and platform/release support. Compare recommendations with observed state and policy before changes. Keep human accountability and independent verification for impactful actions.

##### Worked review check

An AI command is absent from the target image’s parser. What evidence takes precedence?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Use the actual device's command help/parser, supported release documentation and verified operating state. The AI text is an unvalidated suggestion. A command absent from the target image does not become supported because the suggestion looks convincing.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Collect evidence for an AI-assisted operations workflow.

**Covered features:** Generative AI; Predictive AI; Machine learning; Validation.

##### Collect a bounded operational evidence set

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Collect a limited useful evidence set and protect sensitive information.

Use these observations to investigate an anomaly. Redact identities/secrets before sending evidence to an approved assistant. Prediction/generation are functions of an AI/analytics service; no generic IOS enable AI command exists.

```text
show interfaces counters errors
show interfaces status
show processes cpu sorted
show logging | last 30
```


##### Validate an assistant’s suggested change

**Category:** reference. **Platform/context:** Management workstation · commands run outside IOS XE

**In plain language:** Check an assistant’s proposal against device support and actual test results.

Treat output as a proposal. Match commands against the actual device parser/reference, test the hypothesis and validate the result. Machine-learning training/inference commands belong to the selected external service.

```text
# Example prompt template — not a shell or IOS command:
Role: network troubleshooting assistant
Evidence: sanitized interface status and new error-counter growth
Task: rank likely causes; cite the supporting observations
Output: hypotheses, read-only checks, then a proposed change
Constraint: mark uncertainty and platform/version assumptions
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Time series and representative telemetry are needed for useful predictions; one counter snapshot does not establish a trend.
- Do not run a generated configuration merely because its syntax resembles IOS.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The arrows show measurements leading to investigation and a checked change. An anomaly is a reason to investigate, not a final proof of an attack.

```text
Telemetry → anomaly detection → investigate evidence → propose fix → validate → controlled change.
A generated configuration is a draft until its syntax and operational effect are verified.
```


#### Check your understanding

Which is an example of predictive AI in network operations?

- **A.** Forecasting link congestion
- **B.** Creating a prose incident summary
- **C.** Generating a logo
- **D.** Typing a static hostname

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. Forecasting link congestion**

Forecasting congestion estimates a future condition, so it is predictive AI. Producing a new summary or configuration draft is generative AI. Either output still needs comparison with actual evidence.

</details>

Next objective: [6.5 REST API characteristics](#objective-6-5)

<a id="objective-6-5"></a>

### 6.5 — REST API characteristics

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.5/commands)

REST-style APIs expose resources through URLs and use HTTP methods, representations and status codes.

#### In everyday language

An API lets software request information or changes from another system using defined messages. REST-style APIs often use web-style requests.

**A familiar example:** It resembles a service counter with defined request forms: reading a record and changing a record need different forms.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Resource | The item represented by an API address, such as one device. |
| Method | The requested action, such as GET or PATCH. |
| Header | Extra message information, such as content type or credentials. |
| Status code | A response number reporting success or a type of failure. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Build the request.** Select the URL, action, authentication, headers and any body.
2. **Interpret the response.** Read status and returned content: 401 concerns authentication, 403 forbidden access, 429 too many requests.
3. **Verify and respect limits.** Check actual results and honor retry guidance instead of sending requests in a tight loop.

**How to read this:** This is a request/response workflow. HTTPS protects the transport; permission and method meaning still require their own checks.

**Keep this in mind:** Content-Type describes what you send; Accept describes the response format you want.

#### Build your understanding

- GET reads a resource. POST commonly creates or invokes an operation. PUT generally replaces a resource representation; PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes a resource.
- 2xx indicates success; 201 commonly means created; 400 is a bad request; 401 lacks valid authentication; 403 is forbidden; 404 is not found; 429 is rate limited; 5xx indicates a server-side error.
- APIs may use basic authentication over TLS, tokens, API keys or OAuth flows. Use HTTPS, keep credentials out of source code, validate response schemas and handle pagination and rate limits.
- For an ordinary JSON API, Content-Type: application/json describes a JSON request body and Accept: application/json requests a JSON response. These headers do not choose the HTTP operation or authenticate the caller. Follow the actual API specification: model-specific services such as RESTCONF can use a more specific media type, including application/yang-data+json.
- HTTP 429 signals that requests exceed a rate limit. A Retry-After response field, when supplied, gives a delay in seconds or an HTTP date before the next attempt. Honor that guidance and apply suitable backoff or reduced polling rather than retrying in a tight loop. Missing Retry-After does not justify unlimited retries; use the service's documented policy.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 23](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Connect CRUD to HTTP

**Start here:** HTTP methods express different actions. Stateless means each request carries the needed context; it does not mean the server forgets all stored devices or other resources.

GET reads, POST commonly creates/invokes, PUT generally replaces, PATCH partially updates and DELETE removes. Stateless requests contain needed context; statelessness does not forbid stored resources. Idempotence concerns repeated intended effect rather than identical timestamps or responses.

##### Read the whole exchange

**Start here:** Read the complete message: destination, action, identity, format, status and content. Encoding credentials is not encryption; use protected transport and appropriate permissions.

Check URI, method, authentication, headers, encoding, status and body. Accept specifies desired response media; Content-Type describes the sent body. Basic authentication encodes rather than encrypts credentials; TLS supplies transport protection. Tokens still need authorization and careful handling.

##### Worked review check

A valid token receives 403. Is this identical to missing-token 401?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. A 403 normally means the requested access is forbidden under the service policy; a 401 concerns missing or invalid authentication. Check permissions, token scope and the API's specific documented response behavior.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Enable RESTCONF and read a JSON-encoded interface resource.

**Covered features:** Authentication; CRUD/HTTP verbs; Encoding; Status codes.

##### Enable the device RESTCONF endpoint

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Enable the device API with its intended protected management path and identity controls.

Preconfigure a suitable management user/AAA, SSH/HTTPS management policy and a trusted certificate. Restrict TCP 443 to the intended management sources.

```text
enable
configure terminal
restconf
ip http authentication local
ip http secure-server
end
```


##### Read interfaces from a management workstation

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Management workstation · commands run outside IOS XE

**In plain language:** Run the example web request on a management computer, with a verified device certificate.

curl prompts for the password instead of placing it on the command line. The CA certificate must trust the device certificate and the hostname must match. This is HTTP GET; do not type this into IOS.

```text
curl --cacert lab-ca.pem --user apiuser \
  -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  https://sw1.lab.example/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces
```


##### Inspect service health and learn method semantics

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Check API service health and the meaning of each action on the supported resource model.

RESTCONF GET reads; POST creates/invokes; PUT replaces; PATCH modifies; DELETE removes. Use supported YANG resource models and authorization. NETCONF session output does not list every RESTCONF request.

```text
show platform software yang-management process
show netconf-yang sessions
show ip http server status
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- 401: authenticate; 403: inspect authorization; 404: verify path/model; 400: validate payload; 429: respect rate limits.
- NETCONF on TCP 830 and RESTCONF on HTTPS are different protocols.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** GET reads devices in this example. Authorization carries a placeholder token, Accept asks for JSON, 200 reports success, and the JSON body contains an items list.

```text
GET /api/v1/devices
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"items":[{"hostname":"R1","status":"up"}]}
```


#### Check your understanding

Which HTTP method generally makes a partial resource update?

- **A.** GET
- **B.** PATCH
- **C.** DELETE
- **D.** HEAD

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. PATCH**

PATCH requests a partial change to a resource. PUT generally supplies a replacement representation. Use the API's documented format and permissions; neither method name alone proves the resulting network works.

</details>

Next objective: [6.6 Ansible and Terraform capabilities](#objective-6-6)

<a id="objective-6-6"></a>

### 6.6 — Ansible and Terraform capabilities

**Exam target:** Recognize.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.6) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.6/commands)

Configuration-management and infrastructure-as-code tools describe intended state and automate repeatable changes.

#### In everyday language

Ansible and Terraform help describe and apply intended changes, with different ways to organize and track their work.

**A familiar example:** A work list names tasks and targets; a building plan describes the desired result and tracks the objects built.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Ansible’s list of managed hosts and associated values. |
| Playbook | Ansible’s organized tasks for selected hosts. |
| Provider | Terraform’s integration for a particular service or platform. |
| State | Terraform’s stored mapping between configured resources and real objects. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Describe targets and intent.** Choose supported Ansible modules or Terraform providers for the actual platform.
2. **Preview or review the work.** Inspect tasks or a Terraform plan before applying changes.
3. **Apply and verify.** Check results and protect credentials and state, which may contain sensitive values.

**How to read this:** This compares workflows. The tools overlap in some uses but are not identical or universally interchangeable.

**Keep this in mind:** A preview is not an applied change; a completed apply is not independent proof of user service health.

#### Build your understanding

- Ansible commonly uses agentless connections such as SSH or APIs. YAML playbooks describe tasks, inventories identify targets, and modules implement operations.
- Terraform uses declarative configuration and providers to manage infrastructure resources. The plan previews changes; apply executes them; state tracks managed resources.
- Both benefit from version control and review. They are not interchangeable in every use case: select supported modules/providers, protect secrets and state, and validate actual outcomes.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 24](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Compare mechanisms

**Start here:** Ansible organizes targets and tasks; Terraform organizes declared resources with service providers and a stored mapping to real objects. Their workflows can overlap without being identical.

Ansible inventories select targets, variables provide values and playbooks organize module tasks over SSH/APIs. Terraform uses providers and declarative resources: init prepares dependencies, plan previews and apply executes intended changes. Their uses can overlap without identical workflows.

##### Protect state and check convergence

**Start here:** A state file can contain resolved sensitive values even when the configuration uses variables. Protect it, keep credentials controlled and verify real results independently.

Terraform state can contain sensitive resource values and requires controlled storage/access. Both tools need supported modules/providers, controlled secrets and independent verification. Repeating a properly designed intended-state operation should converge; repeating arbitrary commands is not automatically safe.

##### Worked review check

Why is Terraform state sensitive even when configuration uses variables?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

State can store resolved resource attributes, including secret values. Putting a secret behind a variable name in configuration does not ensure it stays out of state. Protect the state file and its storage/access controls accordingly.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Run Ansible/Terraform from a management workstation.

**Covered features:** Ansible inventory/playbooks; Terraform providers/state/plan; Intended-state management.

##### Use Ansible for a read-only IOS command task

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Management workstation · commands run outside IOS XE

**In plain language:** Run a read-only Ansible task from the management computer using the correct inventory and connection settings.

The inventory needs ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli and ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios. Host-key verification and credentials must be configured appropriately. This runs outside the switch.

```text
# After configuring an inventory, SSH auth and cisco.ios collection:
ansible-galaxy collection install cisco.ios
ansible routers -i inventory.yml -m cisco.ios.ios_command \
  -a '{"commands":["show ip interface brief"]}'
```


##### Preview a Terraform project before applying it

**Category:** reference. **Platform/context:** Management workstation · commands run outside IOS XE

**In plain language:** Initialize and preview the reviewed Terraform project before any separate apply decision.

Use a reviewed project with a compatible provider for the actual service/device. init downloads providers; plan may contact infrastructure. apply performs changes and is intentionally a separate decision. Terraform is not an IOS command interpreter.

```text
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan
```


##### Verify the resulting device state independently

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

**In plain language:** Check the changed device itself rather than relying only on the automation tool’s completion message.

Use the specific checks appropriate to the planned change. Keep Terraform state and all automation credentials protected.

```text
show interfaces description
show ip interface brief
show running-config interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Ansible check mode support depends on the module; a command module is primarily for observation.
- A provider/schema for a different platform cannot be assumed to work on IOS XE.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** The indented YAML is an Ansible task using a Cisco module to set a hostname. Terraform init, plan and apply are separate workstation commands, not IOS commands.

```text
Ansible YAML:
- hosts: routers
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: Set hostname
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines: hostname R1

Terraform lifecycle: init → plan → apply
```


#### Check your understanding

Which Terraform operation previews proposed infrastructure changes?

- **A.** plan
- **B.** ping
- **C.** commit-memory
- **D.** discover

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. plan**

terraform plan previews proposed changes by comparing configuration, stored state and observed resources. It is a preview step; terraform apply performs the changes as a separate operation.

</details>

Next objective: [6.7 JSON data components](#objective-6-7)

<a id="objective-6-7"></a>

### 6.7 — JSON data components

**Exam target:** Recognize.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.7) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/6.7/commands)

JSON is a text format used by APIs. Its syntax and data types must be interpreted precisely.

#### In everyday language

JSON is a text format for structured data. Punctuation and quotation marks tell software what each value means.

**A familiar example:** A form distinguishes a checkbox from a text box even when the text box contains the word false.

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Object | Named key/value pairs enclosed in braces { }. |
| Array | An ordered list enclosed in square brackets [ ]. |
| String | Text enclosed in double quotation marks. |
| Boolean/null | Unquoted true or false, and the explicit null value. |

##### Walk through the idea

1. **Locate the container.** Braces mean an object; square brackets mean a list.
2. **Read each value’s type.** 1500 is a number; "1500" is text. false is a boolean; "false" is text.
3. **Follow nested levels.** A list can contain objects. A present null field differs from a missing field.

**How to read this:** This is a reading sequence. JSON does not permit comments, trailing commas, single-quoted strings or undefined.

**Keep this in mind:** Visible words alone are insufficient: quotation marks can change the type.

#### Build your understanding

- Objects use braces and contain double-quoted string keys with colon-separated values. Arrays use square brackets and preserve ordered values.
- JSON values can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays or objects. true, false and null are lowercase and unquoted; a quoted "true" is a string.
- JSON does not support comments or trailing commas. Nested structures represent resources; read each level carefully to distinguish one object from a list of objects.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 23](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Trace each level

**Start here:** Read from the outside inward: object, named field, list, then the item inside it. A number, a boolean and text containing the same characters remain different types.

Objects map double-quoted string keys to values; arrays are ordered. 1500 differs from "1500", and false differs from "false". null is an explicit value rather than an absent key. Read nested structures before interpreting a resource field.

##### Recognize the encoding

**Start here:** JSON has strict punctuation rules and no comments. YAML or XML examples use other formats; valid JSON still needs the API’s field definitions to have the intended meaning.

JSON forbids comments, trailing commas, single-quoted strings and undefined. XML/YAML are alternative serializations; an Ansible YAML example is not JSON merely because both describe structured data. Use the API’s schema to interpret field meanings.

##### Worked review check

In {"ports":[{"up":false}],"gateway":null}, what are the types of ports, up and gateway?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Read the outer object first. ports is an array, marked by square brackets, containing an object. Inside that object, up is the unquoted boolean false. gateway is present with the null value, which differs from an absent field or the text "null".

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Inspect JSON returned by an API on the workstation.

**Covered features:** Objects/keys; Arrays; Strings/numbers; Booleans/null; JSON syntax.

##### Read and validate JSON locally

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Management workstation · commands run outside IOS XE

**In plain language:** Use Python or jq on the management computer to check the JSON and read its fields.

Python and jq run on the management computer, with jq installed for the jq examples. The resource-model wrapper must match the response; a different YANG model changes the JSON path.

```text
# After saving a RESTCONF GET response as interfaces.json:
python -m json.tool interfaces.json
jq keys interfaces.json
jq '.["ietf-interfaces:interfaces"].interface[] | {name, enabled}' interfaces.json
```


##### Recognize the data structure

**Category:** reference. **Platform/context:** JSON example — data, not IOS commands

**In plain language:** Identify the outer object, nested list and boolean values before interpreting the data.

The outer object contains a namespaced key; interface is an array; enabled is a boolean. No trailing commas, comments or single-quoted JSON strings are permitted.

```text
{
  "ietf-interfaces:interfaces": {
    "interface": [
      {"name": "GigabitEthernet1/0/1", "enabled": true}
    ]
  }
}
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- JSON output from an API is different from normal text produced by IOS show commands.
- Do not append an invented | json suffix to a show command unless that exact platform explicitly supports it.

##### Command references

- [Cisco IOS XE programmability documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/iosxe/)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

**How to read the example:** hostname is text, enabled is a boolean and mtu is a number. interfaces is an array containing an object whose ip field is explicitly null.

```text
{
  "hostname": "R1",
  "enabled": true,
  "mtu": 1500,
  "interfaces": [{"name": "Gi0/0", "ip": null}]
}
```


#### Check your understanding

What data type is the value of "interfaces" in {"interfaces":["Gi0/0","Gi0/1"]}?

- **A.** String
- **B.** Boolean
- **C.** Array
- **D.** Number

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**C. Array**

Square brackets identify an array, an ordered list. Here interfaces contains two text strings, Gi0/0 and Gi0/1. Braces would identify an object of named key/value pairs instead.

</details>

<a id="abbreviation-reference"></a>

## Abbreviation reference

The same standalone definitions appear in the site’s glossary and optional dotted term pop-ups. Read the full name alongside the explanation; a technical acronym can describe a specific job rather than an entire working service.

| Abbreviation | Full name | Plain-language explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 802.1Q | IEEE 802.1Q VLAN Tagging | The Ethernet standard that lets a link carry several VLANs while keeping their frames labeled by group. The label identifies the VLAN; it does not encrypt the data or route between groups. |
| 802.1X | IEEE 802.1X Port-Based Network Access Control | A framework for checking a user or device before granting network access. The client asks to join, a switch or AP controls entry, and an authentication service checks the supplied identity evidence. |
| AAA | Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting | Three security jobs: check who someone is, decide what they may do, and record their activity. A successful login does not automatically permit every command or produce every needed audit record. |
| AAAA | IPv6 Address Record | A DNS directory entry containing an IPv6 address for a name. An A record supplies the corresponding IPv4 address type. |
| ACK | Acknowledgment | An acknowledgment confirms receipt. In TCP, the ACK flag and acknowledgment number help track received bytes and participate in connection setup and reliable delivery. |
| ACL | Access Control List | An ordered allow/block rule list. The first matching rule wins; traffic matching none reaches an unstated final deny. The list must be attached to the intended interface or feature to have an effect there. |
| AD | Administrative Distance | A router's preference between different sources offering a route to the same address block. Lower is preferred. This does not override choosing a more specific matching installed route for a packet. |
| AES | Advanced Encryption Standard | An encryption algorithm used to make data unreadable without the appropriate key. It is used inside protection systems such as wireless security and IPsec; selecting a cipher alone does not complete those systems. |
| AH | Authentication Header | An IPsec protection that checks packet integrity and sender origin but does not hide the packet content with encryption. ESP is normally used when encrypted confidentiality is required too. |
| AI | Artificial Intelligence | Software performing tasks such as spotting patterns, predicting events or writing new content. In network operations it can help investigate, but its recommendations still need checking against evidence. |
| AKM | Authentication and Key Management | The wireless security choices controlling how a client proves identity and how keys are established. Shared-key, Enterprise login and SAE are examples with different authentication workflows. |
| AP | Access Point | A device providing a Wi-Fi radio connection to a network. Some APs are configured individually; others join a controller that coordinates their settings and policy. |
| API | Application Programming Interface | A defined way for software to ask another system for information or actions. For example, a management program can request a device list or a configuration change. |
| ARP | Address Resolution Protocol | The local IPv4 lookup asking which MAC address corresponds to a next-hop IP address. The answer helps build the Ethernet delivery frame. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead. |
| AS | Autonomous System | A collection of IP networks operated under a common routing administration and policy. It has an identifying number when participating in routing between autonomous systems. |
| ASIC | Application-Specific Integrated Circuit | A chip designed for a particular job rather than general computing. A switch can use one to forward large amounts of traffic without making its main processor handle every packet. |
| ASN | Autonomous System Number | The number identifying an autonomous system, a group of networks with common routing administration. BGP uses these numbers to describe which routing organizations a path crosses. |
| BDR | Backup Designated Router | The OSPF backup coordinator elected on a segment that uses DR/BDR roles. It is ready to become the designated router if that coordinator fails. |
| BGP | Border Gateway Protocol | A routing protocol used between network organizations and in some large networks. It exchanges destination information and path attributes. Detailed BGP configuration is outside this path's main single-area OSPF focus. |
| BPDU | Bridge Protocol Data Unit | A switch control message used to build and maintain a loop-free Spanning Tree. Receiving or losing these messages can trigger different guard protections. |
| BSS | Basic Service Set | One basic wireless service group. In an ordinary infrastructure Wi-Fi network, it consists of an access-point radio and the clients associated with it. |
| BSSID | Basic Service Set Identifier | The identifier distinguishing a particular wireless service set, commonly using an AP radio's MAC-based identity. It differs from the network name a user selects, called the SSID. |
| CAPWAP | Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points | The communication used between supported lightweight access points and a wireless controller. Control commonly uses UDP 5246; tunneled data commonly uses UDP 5247. |
| CCMP | Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol | AES-based wireless protection that hides data and checks it for unauthorized changes. It is commonly associated with WPA2 and is separate from deciding how users authenticate. |
| CCNA | Cisco Certified Network Associate | Cisco's associate-level networking certification. This website teaches the CCNA 200-301 v1.1 objectives and uses original study questions rather than actual exam questions. |
| CDP | Cisco Discovery Protocol | Cisco's discovery messages for directly connected neighbors. They can describe the device and cable ports, but do not prove a whole route or application works. |
| CEF | Cisco Express Forwarding | Cisco's efficient packet-forwarding system. It uses a forwarding table and next-link delivery information prepared from routing and neighbor information. |
| CIDR | Classless Inter-Domain Routing | Using an explicit /prefix length to describe an address block instead of assuming old address-class boundaries. This permits different subnet sizes and combining suitable routes into larger blocks. |
| CLI | Command-Line Interface | A text-based control panel where you type commands. Cisco devices accept different commands in basic, privileged and configuration modes; the prompt helps identify the current mode. |
| CNAME | Canonical Name Record | A DNS entry making one name an alias of another name. It points to a name rather than directly storing an IPv4 or IPv6 address. |
| CoS | Class of Service | A traffic-priority classification. On an 802.1Q trunk, a three-bit field can label eight priority values. This is different from the six-bit DSCP field inside an IP packet. |
| CPU | Central Processing Unit | The main processor executing system software. Heavy processor use can slow administration or routing decisions even when dedicated forwarding hardware continues carrying traffic. |
| CRC | Cyclic Redundancy Check | A calculation for detecting corrupted information. An Ethernet CRC error means a received frame failed its check; it suggests investigating the physical link and compatible settings, not automatic repair of the data. |
| CRUD | Create, Read, Update, and Delete | Four common data actions: create something, read it, update it or delete it. APIs express these through supported requests; HTTP GET normally performs the read role. |
| CSMA/CA | Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance | Wi-Fi's approach to sharing a channel: devices listen, wait and use coordination to reduce simultaneous transmissions. They still compete for the same airtime, so more devices can reduce each one's available capacity. |
| CSMA/CD | Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection | The older half-duplex Ethernet method that detects competing transmissions on a shared medium. Modern switched full-duplex links let both ends send simultaneously and do not use it to take turns. |
| DAD | Duplicate Address Detection | An IPv6 check asking whether a proposed address is already in use on the local link. It helps detect a conflict before the device uses that address normally. |
| DAI | Dynamic ARP Inspection | A switch check on ARP messages, which claim which MAC belongs to an IPv4 address. It compares claims with trusted bindings or configured policy to help stop false local-address claims. |
| DHCP | Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol | A service assigning device settings, such as an IPv4 address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server, for a lease period. A relay can forward requests when the server is on another network. |
| DHCPv6 | Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 | A service providing IPv6 addresses or other host settings. Default-router discovery normally comes from Router Advertisements instead, so an address assignment alone does not prove a route out exists. |
| DNS | Domain Name System | The network's name directory. It returns records such as the IPv4 or IPv6 address for a website name. It commonly uses UDP and TCP 53; resolving a name does not itself establish the application connection. |
| DORA | Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge | Four common initial DHCPv4 stages: the client discovers service, the server offers settings, the client requests a lease and the server acknowledges it. An offer alone is not the completed assignment. |
| DR | Designated Router | The OSPF coordinator elected for certain shared network segments. It reduces how many full database relationships are needed. An established DR is not automatically replaced by a later higher-priority candidate. |
| DROTHER | Designated Router Other | An OSPF router on a broadcast segment that is neither its designated nor backup designated router. Two such ordinary routers can normally remain 2-Way with each other while being Full with the coordinators. |
| DSCP | Differentiated Services Code Point | A six-bit label in an IP packet used to identify its intended traffic treatment. The label does not create bandwidth; devices must implement the policy that interprets it. |
| DTLS | Datagram Transport Layer Security | Security similar to TLS adapted to message/datagram transport. Supported wireless-controller systems use it to protect CAPWAP control communication. |
| DTP | Dynamic Trunking Protocol | Cisco's automatic trunk-negotiation protocol on supported switch ports. Explicitly configuring the intended access/trunk role can avoid depending on that negotiation. |
| EAP | Extensible Authentication Protocol | A framework carrying different ways to prove identity. Enterprise Wi-Fi commonly uses it between the client, network access device and authentication service rather than one shared Personal-mode passphrase. |
| ECMP | Equal-Cost Multipath | Keeping several eligible next steps with the same route cost. A device can distribute conversations over them; one conversation need not use every path simultaneously. |
| EF | Expedited Forwarding | A traffic treatment intended for suitable delay-sensitive traffic such as voice. Its conventional DSCP label is 46, but actual queue behavior still depends on the device policy. |
| EIGRP | Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol | A routing protocol used within a routing organization. It has its own path-calculation method and score, so its metric is not directly the same unit as OSPF cost. |
| ESP | Encapsulating Security Payload | An IPsec protection carrying selected traffic with services such as encryption and integrity checking, according to the negotiated settings. The chosen protection suite determines which services are supplied. |
| EUI-64 | Extended Unique Identifier, 64-bit | A 64-bit identifier format. Modified EUI-64 can derive an IPv6 interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC by inserting FFFE and flipping one specified bit. Many devices use other identifier methods. |
| FHRP | First-Hop Redundancy Protocol | Protocols providing a shared gateway identity that another physical router can take over. Clients keep one configured gateway while the forwarding device changes after a detected failure. |
| FIB | Forwarding Information Base | A table optimized for forwarding packets, built from selected routing information. It helps the device look up which direction to use for a destination efficiently. |
| FIN | Finish | A TCP flag used to close a connection direction in an orderly way. Each sending direction can finish independently; a reset is a different, abrupt action. |
| FIPS | Federal Information Processing Standards | U.S. federal standards, including standards affecting cryptographic products. A device's FIPS mode can limit which algorithms or commands are permitted. |
| FTP | File Transfer Protocol | A file-transfer protocol with separate command and data connections. Commands commonly use TCP 21; ordinary FTP does not hide credentials or file contents with encryption. |
| Gbps | Gigabits per Second | One billion bits per second, a data rate. Eight bits make one byte, so a gigabit per second is not a gigabyte per second. |
| GHz | Gigahertz | One billion cycles per second, a frequency measurement. A Wi-Fi band labeled in GHz describes radio frequency rather than download speed. |
| GRE | Generic Routing Encapsulation | A tunneling method wrapping one network packet inside another. The wrapper can carry traffic over another network, but GRE by itself does not encrypt the content. |
| GUI | Graphical User Interface | A control panel using screens, forms and buttons instead of only typed commands. A controller GUI exposes configuration objects whose names and menus depend on the product. |
| HSRP | Hot Standby Router Protocol | Cisco's shared-gateway protocol using active and standby routers. Computers use the virtual gateway address while a physical router supplies the active forwarding role. |
| HTTP | Hypertext Transfer Protocol | The web-style request/response protocol also used by many APIs. Plain HTTP does not encrypt the session; HTTPS adds supported security protection. |
| HTTPS | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure | HTTP protected by TLS, with validation of the server's identity. It commonly uses TCP 443; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, commonly UDP 443. Encryption and user permissions are separate checks. |
| ICMP | Internet Control Message Protocol | IP control and error messages, including the echo request/reply used by IPv4 ping. It is separate from TCP and UDP, so a rule allowing those transports does not automatically allow it. |
| ICMPv6 | Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6 | IPv6 control and error messages. It supports ping and essential local-neighbor/router discovery, so indiscriminately blocking it can break normal IPv6 operation. |
| ID | Identifier | A value used to distinguish one thing from another. A VLAN ID labels a logical group; an OSPF router ID identifies a router. The surrounding context determines which object is meant. |
| IEEE | Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers | The standards organization responsible for important networking specifications such as Ethernet, Wi-Fi and VLAN tagging. Its numbered standards describe particular functions, not product model numbers. |
| IGMP | Internet Group Management Protocol | IPv4 messages telling local routers which multicast groups hosts want to receive. A switch can observe those messages to avoid sending group traffic to unnecessary ports. |
| IGP | Interior Gateway Protocol | A routing protocol used within one routing administration rather than between independent organizations. OSPF and EIGRP are examples. |
| IKE | Internet Key Exchange | The negotiation used by IPsec peers to agree on identity, keys and protection settings. Successful negotiation is not proof that the intended user packets are entering the VPN. |
| IKEv2 | Internet Key Exchange Version 2 | A version of the IPsec key-and-identity negotiation protocol. After it succeeds, routes, traffic selection and packet counters still need checking to prove the intended data is protected. |
| IOS | Internetwork Operating System | Cisco's operating-system name used across several generations of network software. The exact command set depends on the device model and installed release. |
| IOS XE | Cisco IOS XE — Internetwork Operating System | Cisco's modular operating system on many switches, routers and wireless controllers. XE is a product designation; commands and features still depend on hardware, software release and licensing. |
| IoT | Internet of Things | Network-connected equipment such as cameras, sensors and industrial devices. These endpoints can need different access limits and maintenance from ordinary user computers. |
| IP | Internet Protocol | Addressing and packet-delivery rules used across networks. IPv4 and IPv6 are separate versions with different address sizes and local-neighbor mechanisms. |
| IPS | Intrusion Prevention System | A security system that analyzes traffic and can stop matching attacks when placed in the traffic path. Detecting an event without an enforcement path is not the same as blocking it. |
| IPsec | Internet Protocol Security | A family of protections for selected IP traffic, often used by VPNs. Peers negotiate security settings; routes and traffic-selection rules decide which packets receive that protection. |
| IPv4 | Internet Protocol Version 4 | The IP version using 32-bit addresses, normally written as four decimal numbers. A mask or /prefix separates the network group from the address positions within it. |
| IPv6 | Internet Protocol Version 6 | The IP version using 128-bit addresses written with hexadecimal digits and colons. It uses local Neighbor Discovery and multicast groups rather than IPv4's ARP/broadcast behavior. |
| IS-IS | Intermediate System to Intermediate System | A routing protocol that builds a map of links to calculate paths inside an organization. It is used in some provider networks; detailed configuration is outside this path's OSPF-focused practice. |
| ISL | Inter-Switch Link | An older Cisco way to carry VLAN information over trunks. The current Catalyst examples use standard 802.1Q tagging instead; do not assume legacy syntax applies to new switches. |
| JSON | JavaScript Object Notation | A text format for structured data. Braces hold named fields; square brackets hold lists. Quoted text, numbers, true/false and null are distinct types. Comments and trailing commas are not allowed. |
| L2 | Layer 2 — Data Link Layer | The local-delivery layer, including Ethernet frames, MAC addresses and VLAN switching. Delivering across different IP networks requires the separate routing function at Layer 3. |
| L3 | Layer 3 — Network Layer | The addressing-and-routing layer used to move packets between IP networks. A routing-capable switch can perform this job as well as local Layer 2 switching. |
| LACP | Link Aggregation Control Protocol | A standard protocol negotiating a bundle of compatible links. Active starts the conversation and passive responds; two passive ends both wait. Other member settings must also agree. |
| LAG | Link Aggregation Group | Several compatible physical connections acting as one logical bundle. Total capacity and resilience can improve, but one conversation normally uses one member connection. |
| LAN | Local Area Network | A network in a local area such as an office. VLANs can divide its switches into separate logical local groups, each with its own broadcast scope. |
| LLDP | Link Layer Discovery Protocol | A multi-vendor standard for directly connected devices to advertise identities and port information. It helps document a cable connection without proving a whole routed path works. |
| LLQ | Low Latency Queuing | A queueing method giving bounded priority to suitable time-sensitive traffic, often voice. Limiting that priority class helps keep other traffic from being starved. |
| LSA | Link-State Advertisement | An OSPF item describing part of the network's link information. Routers collect these items to build the map used for path calculations. |
| LSDB | Link-State Database | The collected link-state map used by a routing protocol such as OSPF. It is information for calculating paths, not just the final list of selected routes. |
| MAC | Media Access Control | Media Access Control is part of local-link networking. An Ethernet MAC address identifies a local sender or receiver; switches learn senders and use receiver addresses for delivery within a VLAN. |
| Mbps | Megabits per Second | One million bits per second, a data rate. It measures how fast information moves rather than how much a file contains; eight bits make one byte. |
| MD5 | Message-Digest Algorithm 5 | An older hashing algorithm with known weaknesses. Recognize it in legacy material, but use supported stronger alternatives where current platform policy requires them. |
| MFA | Multifactor Authentication | Identity checking using different kinds of evidence, such as a password you know and a security key you possess. Two passwords or a password plus PIN remain the same knowledge category. |
| MIB | Management Information Base | The organized set of values a management agent can expose, such as interface counters. Each value has an identifier so a monitoring system can request the right one. |
