| ML | Machine Learning | Methods learning patterns from data to make classifications or predictions. A baseline that omits normal busy periods can produce false alarms; results need context and verification. |
| MQC | Modular QoS Command-Line Interface | Cisco's framework for grouping traffic, defining its treatment and attaching the policy to a supported interface. A policy definition alone does not make traffic pass through it. |
| MTU | Maximum Transmission Unit | The maximum IP packet size a link can carry without fragmentation. Incompatible sizes can break application traffic or routing database exchanges even while small messages get through. |
| MX | Mail Exchange | A DNS entry identifying the mail servers for a domain and their preference values. It is different from directly storing a host's IPv4 or IPv6 address. |
| NA | Neighbor Advertisement | An IPv6 message providing neighbor address information, often answering a Neighbor Solicitation. It helps identify the local delivery address for an IPv6 neighbor. |
| NAT | Network Address Translation | Rewriting IP addresses as traffic crosses a boundary. Fixed mappings, address pools and port sharing work differently; translation by itself is neither encryption nor a complete access-control policy. |
| NDP | Neighbor Discovery Protocol | IPv6's local discovery functions using ICMPv6 messages. They help find neighbors, learn router information and perform other checks on a local link. |
| NETCONF | Network Configuration Protocol | A protocol for software to read or change modeled network settings. It commonly uses SSH on TCP 830 and needs appropriate identity, permissions and management reachability. |
| NGFW | Next-Generation Firewall | A firewall adding checks such as application identity and threat inspection to basic packet filtering. Its actual policy and placement determine what traffic is allowed or stopped. |
| NMS | Network Management System | A platform used to monitor or administer network devices, for example by asking for SNMP counters and collecting events. It is the management system, not a forwarding route. |
| NS | Neighbor Solicitation | An IPv6 local-neighbor request, used for jobs such as finding a neighbor's delivery information and checking whether an address is already in use. |
| NTP | Network Time Protocol | A protocol for synchronizing clocks, commonly over UDP 123. Matching timestamps help relate events across devices, but all clients can still follow an inaccurate reference source. |
| OID | Object Identifier | The structured name of one managed value, such as an interface counter exposed through SNMP. It tells the agent which value is requested; it is not a packet's destination address. |
| OS | Operating System | The software managing hardware and supporting applications. A network operating system also supplies device-specific configuration and monitoring functions. |
| OSI | Open Systems Interconnection | A seven-layer reference model for networking jobs, from physical signals up to applications. The layers are physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. |
| OSPF | Open Shortest Path First | A routing protocol in which routers share link information and calculate paths using costs. This path's configuration work focuses on IPv4 OSPFv2 within one area. |
| OSPFv2 | Open Shortest Path First Version 2 | The OSPF version used here for IPv4. Neighbors exchange a link map, calculate costs and, on applicable shared segments, elect designated and backup coordinator routers. |
| OSPFv3 | Open Shortest Path First Version 3 | An OSPF version originally designed for IPv6. Some supported implementations also carry other address families; exact configuration depends on the platform. |
| PAgP | Port Aggregation Protocol | Cisco's proprietary protocol for negotiating EtherChannel bundles. LACP is the multi-vendor standard emphasized in this Learning Path, and uses different negotiation modes. |
| PAT | Port Address Translation | Translation allowing many inside conversations to share an outside IPv4 address by tracking transport-port information. Cisco's overload keyword commonly enables this behavior. |
| PC | Personal Computer | A general-purpose user computer. Its own address, subnet boundary, gateway, DNS and firewall settings can prevent access even when network equipment is working. |
| PDU | Protocol Data Unit | The name for a piece of information at a particular protocol layer. An Ethernet frame and an IP packet are examples at different layers, rather than interchangeable names for the same wrapper. |
| PKI | Public Key Infrastructure | The system of certificates, keys, trusted issuers and procedures used to establish digital identity. Certificates must be checked against the expected identity, not merely accepted because one was presented. |
| PMF | Protected Management Frames | Protection for selected important Wi-Fi management messages, helping prevent certain forged management actions. WPA3 requires it; it is separate from ordinary user-data encryption. |
| PoE | Power over Ethernet | Power supplied to compatible equipment over Ethernet cabling. Both the individual port capability and the switch's total available watts must meet demand. |
| PPP | Point-to-Point Protocol | A protocol for a connection between two endpoints, providing link setup and carrying network-layer traffic. It is a link-level function, not an IP routing protocol. |
| PPPoE | Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet | Carrying PPP sessions inside Ethernet, used by some broadband access services. It adds a session mechanism over the Ethernet connection. |
| PSK | Pre-Shared Key | A secret shared in advance by the participants. WPA2-Personal uses this model; the ordinary passphrase input and a raw hexadecimal key are different formats. |
| PTR | Pointer Record | A DNS entry for reverse lookup, from an IP address toward a name. A successful reverse answer is separate from forward A/AAAA lookup and application reachability. |
| PVST+ | Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus | Cisco Spanning Tree running a separate loop-prevention instance for each VLAN. Different VLANs can therefore have different chosen root switches and active paths. |
| QoS | Quality of Service | Rules for treating traffic when it competes for limited capacity. They can identify, label, prioritize, drop or delay packets, but cannot create extra physical bandwidth. |
| RA | Router Advertisement | An IPv6 router message announcing information such as local prefixes and whether the router offers a default exit. A host normally learns its default router from suitable RAs rather than DHCPv6. |
| RADIUS | Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service | An identity-service protocol commonly used for network admission. Typical ports are UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for activity accounting. |
| RAM | Random Access Memory | A device's working memory while it runs. Active settings and saved startup settings are separate; saving validated configuration is needed when it should survive reboot. |
| REST | Representational State Transfer | An architectural style often used for APIs. Requests identify resources and use actions such as HTTP GET to read them, with defined representations and response codes. |
| RESTCONF | RESTCONF — REST-Based Network Configuration Protocol | A web-style protocol for reading and changing network data described by YANG models. IOS XE commonly provides it through HTTPS; it is different from a generic arbitrary JSON endpoint. |
| RF | Radio Frequency | Radio signals used for wireless communication. Walls, noise, competing transmitters and antenna placement affect whether devices can hear one another reliably. |
| RFC | Request for Comments | A publication in the Internet technical document series. For example, RFC 1918 defines the three familiar private IPv4 address blocks. |
| RIP | Routing Information Protocol | A routing protocol that scores paths by hop count. Its default administrative distance can appear in route-source comparisons; detailed configuration is outside this path's OSPF focus. |
| RPVST+ | Rapid Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus | Cisco's rapid loop-prevention process running separately for each VLAN. Rapid refers to how quickly it can adapt; a redundant link can still intentionally be kept from forwarding. |
| RRM | Radio Resource Management | Wireless functions coordinating settings such as channel choice and transmit power. Their operation supports a radio design rather than guaranteeing every client has unlimited capacity. |
| RSA | Rivest–Shamir–Adleman | A public-key cryptographic algorithm. A device can use an RSA key pair for functions such as SSH server identity; the public and private keys have different roles. |
| RST | Reset | A TCP flag abruptly resetting or rejecting a connection. It differs from the orderly finish signaled with FIN. |
| RSTP | Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol | A faster form of Spanning Tree that prevents local switching loops. Its main states are discarding, learning and forwarding, describing whether frames are held or allowed through. |
| RTT | Round-Trip Time | The time for a message to reach a destination and for its reply to come back. A ping result therefore measures the round trip, not just one direction. |
| RX | Receive | Receive: traffic arriving at an interface or the receive side of a transceiver. TX is the corresponding send/transmit direction. |
| SA | Security Association | A set of agreed security settings for protected communication. IKE negotiation and IPsec traffic protection maintain distinct associations, so negotiated status and actual protected counters are different checks. |
| SAE | Simultaneous Authentication of Equals | The password-based key exchange used by WPA3-Personal. It is designed to improve resistance to guessing passwords offline from a captured exchange, while strong secrets and correct implementations remain important. |
| SCP | Secure Copy Protocol | A file-transfer protocol using SSH protection. Check the server's identity and permissions; SCP and SFTP are different protocols despite both using SSH. |
| SD-WAN | Software-Defined Wide Area Network | Software-coordinated policy and management for connections between distant sites over supported transports. The real underlying links still provide the capacity and reachability. |
| SDN | Software-Defined Networking | Separating or abstracting network decisions and exposing software interfaces for control. A logically centralized design can use multiple controller servers, and user packets need not all cross one controller. |
| SFP | Small Form-Factor Pluggable | A modular transceiver form used by network equipment. The actual supported signal standard, cable type, wavelength and distance matter; two plugs fitting does not prove a compatible link. |
| SFTP | SSH File Transfer Protocol | A file-transfer protocol carried through SSH. It is distinct from SCP and from ordinary FTP with or without added TLS protection. |
| SLAAC | Stateless Address Autoconfiguration | A way for an IPv6 host to form its own address from router-advertised prefix information. It does not require a DHCPv6 server to assign that address; other host settings still follow the design. |
| SNMP | Simple Network Management Protocol | A monitoring protocol for asking devices for managed values and, when permitted, changing some of them. Polling commonly uses UDP 161; event notifications commonly use UDP 162. |
| SNMPv1 | Simple Network Management Protocol Version 1 | An early monitoring-protocol version using a shared community value for access. It lacks the modern identity and encrypted-content protections available in properly configured SNMPv3. |
| SNMPv2c | Simple Network Management Protocol Version 2c | A community-based SNMP version supporting functions such as retrieving batches of values. Its community string does not encrypt the exchange or provide SNMPv3-style privacy. |
| SNMPv3 | Simple Network Management Protocol Version 3 | An SNMP version with selectable authentication and privacy protection. authPriv provides both authenticated messages and encrypted content; choosing v3 alone does not specify that full protection level. |
| SNR | Signal-to-Noise Ratio | How strong the desired signal is compared with background noise. A clearer signal relative to noise generally supports more reliable wireless communication, separately from security settings. |
| SOHO | Small Office/Home Office | A small-office/home-office environment, often using one box for routing, switching, Wi-Fi and security. Those logical jobs still exist even when they share hardware. |
| SSH | Secure Shell | An encrypted remote-access protocol, commonly TCP 22. A Cisco SSH service needs reachable management addressing, server keys, user authentication and the intended remote-login rules. |
| SSID | Service Set Identifier | The wireless network name people select. Several access-point radios can advertise the same name without proving that their encryption, VLAN or authentication policies match. |
| SSL | Secure Sockets Layer | An older predecessor to TLS. Obsolete SSL versions should not be treated as modern secure HTTPS; supported TLS versions provide current protection. |
| STP | Spanning Tree Protocol | Switch loop prevention that keeps a safe set of links forwarding while redundant paths remain available. In cable descriptions the initials can also mean shielded twisted pair; this site usually means Spanning Tree. |
| SVI | Switch Virtual Interface | A switch's logical IP interface for a VLAN. It can manage the switch or act as that VLAN's gateway when routing is supported and enabled; the VLAN also needs a suitable active forwarding connection. |
| SYN | Synchronize | A TCP flag starting sequence-number synchronization during connection setup. The familiar opening exchange is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. |
| TACACS+ | Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus | An identity/permission/accounting protocol often used to administer network devices and authorize commands. It normally uses TCP 49 and can separate those AAA functions. |
| TCP | Transmission Control Protocol | A transport protocol that sets up a connection, numbers bytes, confirms receipt and resends missing data for reliable ordered delivery. Reliability by itself does not encrypt the content. |
| TFTP | Trivial File Transfer Protocol | A simple file-transfer protocol with no built-in login authentication or encryption. Its initial request normally uses UDP 69, followed by the transfer's own UDP ports. |
| TKIP | Temporal Key Integrity Protocol | An older wireless protection introduced with WPA as a transition from WEP. Recognize it in legacy material; use supported stronger modern wireless protection for current deployments. |
| TLS | Transport Layer Security | Protection for an application conversation, including encryption and supported identity checking. It underpins modern HTTPS; clients still need to validate the intended server and their permissions. |
| TTL | Time to Live | For IPv4, a counter reduced by routers to stop a packet circulating forever. In DNS, the same initials mean how long a record may be cached; those are different timers in different contexts. |
| TX | Transmit | Transmit: traffic sent by an interface or the sending side of a transceiver. RX is the corresponding receive direction. |
| UDP | User Datagram Protocol | A transport protocol sending datagrams without TCP's built-in connection, delivery confirmation or ordering guarantees. An application can add its own checks and retries when needed. |
| URI | Uniform Resource Identifier | A string identifying a resource. A URL is a kind of URI that also indicates where or how to access it, such as a web address. |
| URL | Uniform Resource Locator | An access address such as an HTTPS web link. In an API it commonly identifies the resource to read or change; the method and permissions determine the action. |
| USM | User-Based Security Model | An SNMPv3 security model using users and keys to supply the selected authentication and privacy services. The configured protection level determines whether content is encrypted. |
| UTP | Unshielded Twisted Pair | Copper cable made from twisted wire pairs without an overall shield. Its cable category and Ethernet standard determine suitable speeds and reach. |
| VLAN | Virtual Local Area Network | A logical local Ethernet group kept separate from other groups. Devices in the same VLAN can switch locally; different VLAN subnets need routing and permission for the intended traffic. |
| VLSM | Variable-Length Subnet Mask | Using differently sized IP subnets in one address plan. Fit larger requirements first, align each block correctly and avoid assigning any address range to two groups. |
| VM | Virtual Machine | A software-created computer running its own guest operating system under a hypervisor. Containers normally share a host kernel instead, giving a different kind of isolation. |
| VPN | Virtual Private Network | A logical connection between users or sites over another network. Whether it is encrypted depends on the technology; this path's IPsec VPN examples protect selected traffic between their VPN endpoints. |
| VRF | Virtual Routing and Forwarding | A separate route list and forwarding context inside one shared device. Groups can reuse addresses when the design keeps their route decisions separate; communication between them needs deliberate configuration. |
| VRRP | Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol | A standard shared-gateway protocol allowing a different physical router to take over the virtual identity. Clients keep their gateway setting while the active forwarding role changes. |
| VTEP | VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint | The edge point that adds or removes VXLAN tunnel wrapping. The transport network still needs to carry the resulting packets between those endpoints. |
| VTY | Virtual Teletype | A logical remote-terminal connection on an IOS-style device. Its settings choose login behavior and allowed transports such as SSH; it is not a physical cable socket. |
| VXLAN | Virtual Extensible Local Area Network | Wrapping that carries logical Ethernet segments across a routed IP transport network. It is an overlay tunnel mechanism, different from an ordinary 802.1Q VLAN tag on a local trunk. |
| WAN | Wide Area Network | Connections joining geographically separated sites using provider or Internet services. Its capacity, routing responsibility and encryption depend on the selected service and design. |
| WEP | Wired Equivalent Privacy | An obsolete wireless security mechanism with serious weaknesses. It is useful to recognize historically but should not protect a current wireless deployment. |
| WLC | Wireless LAN Controller | A controller coordinating compatible access points and wireless policy. Catalyst 9800 and older AireOS families use different configuration objects and menus. |
| WMM | Wi-Fi Multimedia | Wi-Fi traffic treatment using categories such as voice, video, best effort and background. It helps devices prioritize access to shared airtime rather than creating extra radio capacity. |
| WPA | Wi-Fi Protected Access | A wireless security family introduced after WEP. Original WPA commonly used the transitional TKIP protection; it should not be confused with newer WPA2/WPA3 mechanisms. |
| WPA2 | Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 | A wireless security generation commonly using AES-CCMP data protection. Personal uses a pre-shared key; Enterprise uses an authentication framework and service instead of one shared Personal passphrase. |
| WPA3 | Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 | A newer wireless security generation. WPA3-Personal uses SAE and WPA3 requires protected management frames; client compatibility and transition settings affect the protection actually negotiated. |
| WRED | Weighted Random Early Detection | A queue-management method that can drop selected packets before the queue fills, using supported traffic-class thresholds. Early drops can encourage responsive senders to slow down. |
| XML | Extensible Markup Language | A structured text format using markup tags. NETCONF uses XML messages; it is a different representation from JSON objects or YAML indentation. |
| YAML | YAML Ain’t Markup Language | A human-readable structured-data format often used for Ansible tasks and configuration files. Indentation groups related information and must be kept correct; YAML is not JSON. |
| YANG | Yet Another Next Generation | A language defining the names, structure and types of network settings and state. Protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF use those models to describe what data may be read or changed. |
| ZTP | Zero-Touch Provisioning | Initial device setup automated through a supported bootstrap process. It reduces manual work but still needs suitable network services, trusted inputs and verification of the resulting configuration. |
